records.themeTitle: Dew and the recovery of an original root
records.themeSummary: Abraham fears that his years before recognizing God remain a permanent stain. Rav Tzadok asks why the image of dew can answer that fear.

records.originEnglish: The Shabbat day meal is the meal of Atika, as stated in the holy Zohar, and the Ari, of blessed memory, associated it with the holiness of Abraham our father. Bereishit Rabbah 39 teaches: “Yours is the dew of your youth”—because our father Abraham was afraid and said, “Might I still bear sin because I worshipped idols all those years?” The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: “Yours is the dew of your youth. Just as this dew flies away, so your sins fly away; just as this dew is a sign of blessing,” and so on. We must understand what answer the blessed God gave him, specifically through the comparison to dew, to set his mind at rest.

records.targetEnglish: The foundation of Abraham our father’s level is that he was the first of the converts, as they said in Chagigah 3a. Only afterward, once Isaac was born and included within him, did he attain the name “Eitan the native,” to be like a native in Israel. The blessed God promised him, “Yours is the dew of your youth,” as stated in Bereishit Rabbah 39: “Might I bear sin?” and so forth. They interpreted “from the womb of the world”: in truth, Abraham our father too was holy from the womb and from the beginning of the world’s creation; only his beginning had been that of a convert. Afterward, however, he merited to reveal his root as the father of the world and the root of the entire Israelite people. He is the beginning of this lineage, the root of Israel, which can change what preceded it as well.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin develops the very reassurance quoted here. Abraham initially appears as a convert, yet his later inclusion of Israel reveals a holy root that precedes that beginning. Dew therefore signifies more than forgetting an embarrassing past: the later revelation reaches back to the root. This prepares Lech Lecha’s account of repentance from love without replacing its required return.

records.themeTitle: The light concealed within dew
records.themeSummary: The dew that revives the dead is connected to the primordial light hidden for those who labor in Oral Torah. Hiddenness does not mean that the source of life has ceased.
records.originHebrew: אַךְ בְּרוֹב הַמְּקוֹמוֹת שֶׁנֶּזְכַּר טַל נִדְרָשׁ עַל טַלָּא דְעַתִּיקָא, כְּמוֹ "מִטַּל הַשָּׁמַיִם", דְּאִיתָא (זֹהַר חֵלֶק א, קמג עַמּוּד ב): "דָּא טַל עִלָּאָה דְּנָגֵיד מֵעַתִּיק יוֹמִין וְכוּלֵי"; וְכֵן "כִּי טַל אוֹרֹת טַלֶּךָ" נִדְרָשׁ בַּגְּמָרָא (כְּתוּבּוֹת קיא עַמּוּד א): "כָּל הַמִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּאוֹר תּוֹרָה, אוֹר תּוֹרָה מְחַיֵּיהוּ וְכוּלֵי", וְהַיְינוּ טַל שֶׁעָתִיד בּוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְהַחֲיוֹת אֶת הַמֵּתִים (שֶׁבַּגְּמָרָא שַׁבָּת פח עַמּוּד ב), וְהוּא טַלָּא דְעַתִּיקָא מֵאוֹר הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁנִּגְנַז לְעַמְלֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (מִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא נֹחַ); וּבַתִּקּוּנִים מַיְיתֵי בֶּאֱמֶת: "כָּל הָעוֹסֵק בְּטַל תּוֹרָה, טַל תּוֹרָה מְחַיֵּיהוּ".
records.originEnglish: Yet in most places where dew is mentioned, it is interpreted as the dew of Atika. Thus, concerning “from the dew of heaven,” the Zohar (I, 143b) says: “This is the supernal dew that flows from the Ancient of Days,” and so forth. Likewise, “For Your dew is a dew of lights” is interpreted in the Talmud (Ketubot 111a): “Whoever makes use of the light of Torah, the light of Torah revives him,” and so forth. This is the dew with which the Holy One, blessed be He, will revive the dead, mentioned in Shabbat 88b. It is the dew of Atika, from the first light that was hidden for those who labor in Oral Torah, as stated in Midrash Tanchuma, Noach. The Tikkunim indeed gives the wording: “Whoever engages in the dew of Torah, the dew of Torah revives him.”

records.targetEnglish: The Talmud begins with tractate Berakhot—with the mitzvot of reciting the Shema, prayer, and blessings, which are speech directly addressed to the blessed God and a clear recognition of His reality. This resembles “A maidservant saw at the sea,” and so forth: at the beginning, when a Jew begins to approach words of Torah, the blessed God opens a great light for him. As stated in Shabbat 88b: after their souls departed at the first utterance, the Holy One, blessed be He, brought out the dew with which He will revive the dead and restored them to life. The first utterance opens a great light; afterward He brings down dew, which dims the light. Dew appears only when there is no sunlight, as it says, “When the sun grew hot, it melted.” Yet with the blessed God, “Your dew is a dew of lights”: it is full of the light with which He will revive the dead. The explanation is that the Sages said, “Faithfulness”—this is the order Zeraim. Faith is needed when something is not clear to the eye and one must believe, as in “Your faithfulness at night”; by day it is called truth, because it is clear to the eye. Although a great light seems to open at the beginning, the blessed God has profound depths, light above light, beside which that first light is darkness. He wishes to raise a person ever higher. As soon as the person moves beyond the beginning, this light becomes familiar to him and returns to a state of darkness and faith.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim explains the otherwise puzzling combination of dew, dimness, and life-giving light. A first disclosure becomes concealed as a person is raised toward a higher light; what appears dark to the recipient remains full of light with God. This gives a concrete account of why the dew of resurrection can also describe the hidden Torah light in Lech Lecha.

records.targetHebrew: וכן יראה השי"ת לעתיד, שכל נפשות ישראל הכירו תמיד זה החיבור, כי היה להם תמיד רעותא טבא להתמשך אחר רצונו ית', אשר מזה יהיה באמת אז כל התחיה. וממילא יתברר אז גם למפרע שלא היה מעולם שום מחיצה בין העליונים לתחתונים. ולזה איתא בש"ס (כתובות קיא:) כל המשתמש באור תורה אור תורה מחייהו, וכל שאינו משתמש באור תורה אין אור תורה מחייהו, היינו כי אור תורה רומז על החיבור מהשי"ת לישראל, שמזה יהיה כל התחיה, ומי שאינו מאמין בזה האור החיבור מהיכן יהיה לו תחיה לעתיד והתחיה לעתיד יהיה כמו שהמשיל כבוד אזמו"ר זללה"ה את הישועה שיהיה לעתיד, מאחי יוסף, שהיה נדמה להם שהם עומדים לפני מלך עכו"ם ומתוכחים עמו והמה עומדים בסכנת נפשות. ואח"כ נתגלה להם שלא היה להם שום סכנות, כי לפני אחיהם היו עומדים. כך יתגלה לעתיד התחיית המתים שלא היה מעולם שום מחיצה, כענין הכתוב (זכריה י׳:ו׳) והיה כאשר לא זנחתים.
records.targetEnglish: So too, the blessed God will show in the future that all the souls of Israel always recognized this bond, because they always had a good desire to be drawn after His will. From this, all the resurrection will indeed arise. It will therefore become clear retrospectively that there was never any barrier between the upper and lower realms. Thus the Talmud (Ketubot 111b) says: “Whoever makes use of the light of Torah, the light of Torah revives him; whoever does not make use of the light of Torah, the light of Torah does not revive him.” The light of Torah signifies the bond from the blessed God to Israel, from which all resurrection will arise. If someone does not believe in this light of connection, from where will he have resurrection in the future? The future resurrection will resemble the example my revered grandfather, of blessed memory, gave for the future salvation: Joseph’s brothers thought they were standing before a gentile king and arguing with him, with their lives in danger. Afterward it was revealed that they had not been in danger, for they were standing before their own brother. So too, the resurrection will reveal in the future that there was never any barrier, in the sense of the verse, “They shall be as though I had not forsaken them.”
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef interprets the same teaching about Torah’s reviving light as the enduring bond between God and Israel, expressed in the desire to follow His will. His example of Joseph’s brothers explains how a hidden bond can later be recognized as having existed throughout. This clarifies the life-bearing quality of Rav Tzadok’s hidden light.

records.themeTitle: Continuing ascent after genuine attainment
records.themeSummary: Abraham’s love expresses itself in continual movement from one level to another. A real attainment does not end the work of a living person.

records.originEnglish: The quality of all the Patriarchs was exertion in the service of the blessed God, as stated in Sanhedrin 96a: “When I pay the reward of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who ran before Me like horses,” and so on. This was especially true of Abraham our father, whose occupation was the holiness of positive commandments, rooted in love and alacrity. As they said in Chullin 16a, “The verse teaches us Abraham’s alacrity.” He never became still or rested from exerting himself in action in the service of the blessed God. This is what was said to him: “Go for yourself”—to set your own level right, as stated in the holy Zohar. He was to keep moving from level to level in his quality of love. This corresponds to reaching the passage “You shall love.”
records.targetHebrew: פְּעָמִים נִדְמֶה לָאָדָם שֶׁכְּבָר שָׁב וְנִמְחֲלוּ חֲטָאָיו, וְאַחַר זְמַן חוֹזֵר וּמִתְעוֹרֵר לְהִתְמַרְמֵר עַל חֲטָאָיו וּמַרְגִּישׁ שֶׁשְּׁנֵי הַמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת אֵינָם דִּמְיוֹן. וּבֶאֱמֶת שְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, דְּקַיְימָא לַן (יוֹמָא פו:): עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁהִתְוַדָּה יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים זֶה, חוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הַבָּא, וַאֲפִילּוּ בַּעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁהַהֲלָכָה דְּלֹא זָז מִשָּׁם עַד שֶׁמּוֹחֲלִין לוֹ, וַהֲרֵי גַּם זֶה אֱמֶת. רַק כְּמוֹ שֶׁאֵין שִׁיעוּר לְכָל מַעֲלוֹת הָאָדָם בְּמַדְרֵגָתוֹ, כָּךְ אֵין שִׁיעוּר לְמַדְרֵגוֹת הַתְּשׁוּבָה. וּכְפִי מַעֲלַת הָאָדָם וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ, כָּךְ הוּא תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ. כִּי כָּל עִנְיְנֵי הָאָדָם עַל יַחַס אֶחָד, וְהָאָדָם אֵינוֹ עוֹמֵד בְּמָקוֹם אֶחָד, כִּי עַל זֶה נִתְאוֹנֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם קוֹדֶם פְּטִירָתוֹ: "לֹא אוּכַל עוֹד וְגוֹמֵר", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "בַּמֵּתִים חָפְשִׁי", וְנִקְרָא "נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ", אֲבָל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין נָח לְעוֹלָם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין הוּא מַרְגִּישׁ. וְכָל מִי שֶׁשָּׁרְשׁוֹ טוֹב דִּגְמִירֵי דְּלָא הָוֵי בִּישָׁא, הוּא הוֹלֵךְ מִמַּעֲלָה לְמַעֲלָה בְּטוֹבָה, וְכֵן לְהֵיפֶךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: זִקְנֵי תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים כָּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּזְקִינִין וְכוּלֵי, זִקְנֵי עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ וְכוּלֵי. וּלְכָךְ כְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ אֶל מַעֲלָה וּמַדְרֵגָה יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה, אָז כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָה זוֹ לֹא הִתְחִיל לָשׁוּב עֲדַיִן, וְחַטָּאתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ תָּמִיד מִדַּרְגָּא לְדַרְגָּא וּכְשֶׁהוּא בַּמַּדְרֵגָה הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה כְּבָר תִּיקֵּן כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ הַחֵטְא וְכֵן בְּכָל דַּרְגִּין וְעוֹלָמוֹת וְאֵין עוֹד רֹשֶׁם; וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּשֶׁמִּתְעַלֶּה, חוֹזֵר הַחֵטְא בְּכָל תָּקְפּוֹ, וְדָבָר זֶה עָמוֹק בַּחָכְמָה.
records.targetEnglish: Sometimes a person thinks that he has already repented and his sins have been forgiven. After a time, he again feels stirred to bitterness over his sins, and he senses that neither thought is imaginary. In truth, both are true. We rule that sins confessed on one Yom Kippur are confessed again on the next—even transgressions for which the law is that one does not leave that place before being forgiven. That too is true. Just as there is no limit to a person’s higher levels, there is no limit to the levels of repentance. His repentance corresponds to his level and understanding, for all his affairs stand in proportion to one another. A person does not stand in one place. This is what Moses lamented before his passing: “I can no longer,” and so on. As it says, “Free among the dead,” and one who dies is described as having rested his soul; but in this world there is never rest, even if the person does not feel it. Whoever has a good root, of which we have a tradition that it will not become bad, goes from level to level in goodness; and the reverse is likewise so, as stated about aged Torah scholars and aged unlearned people. Therefore, when he reaches a greater level, he has not yet begun to repent in the measure of that level, and his sin remains before him from level to level. At the lower level, he had already repaired the sin according to his level, and likewise in all the corresponding levels and worlds, leaving no trace. Yet when he rises, the sin returns in all its force. This is a profound matter of wisdom.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik makes the continuing movement precise: a person may have truly repaired a fault at one level, yet a higher level calls for a deeper return. This illuminates the active, loving ascent in Rav Tzadok’s account of Abraham. It addresses that moving side of the paragraph; it does not erase the separate standing recognition of Divine unity described immediately afterward.

records.themeTitle: Alacrity governed by a known Divine will
records.themeSummary: The Patriarchs’ running is an image of devoted action. Its worth depends on what directs the speed.

records.targetHebrew: סוס ורוכבו רמה בים. ביאר בזה אאזמו"ר הגה"ק זללה"ה סוס רומז על מהירות. ורוכב רומז על ישוב הדעת. ובעכו"ם אין חפץ ה' לא במהירות ולא בישוב הדעת שלהם כי אחר שמסתעף מהרוכב מהירות כ"כ באין מעצור לרוחם לזה שניהם רמה בים. ואף שבישראל חביב אף המהירות שלהם כדאי' בילקוט (מלכים ב' רמז רמ"ד) אמר הקב"ה ומה בשכר פסיעות ששלמתי לאותו רשע שרץ אחר כבודי אתה תמה כשאני משלם שכר לאברהם ליצחק וליעקב שרצו לפני כסוסים על אחת כמה וכמה. אכן בישראל הוא כענין שנאמר (תהילים ס״ח:ה׳) סולו לרוכב בערבות ביה שמו. ובספר (ישעי' כ"ו) בטחו בה' עדי עד כי ביה ה' צור עולמים. לזה בעת שמפורש לפניהם רצון השי"ת אז עושים במהירות בלי ישוב הדעת מצדם. אבל מהירות האומות הוא רק להתפשט בלי דעת לזה אין ה' חפץ בהם אף לא בישוב הדעת שלהם:
records.targetEnglish: “Horse and rider He hurled into the sea.” My holy grandfather, of blessed memory, explained: the horse signifies speed, and the rider signifies settled judgment. Among the idolaters, God desires neither their speed nor their settled judgment. Since such unrestrained speed issues from the rider, both are hurled into the sea. In Israel, however, even their speed is beloved. As the Yalkut says: the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “If you are astonished at the reward of the steps I paid that wicked man who ran for My honor, how much more so when I pay the reward of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who ran before Me like horses!” Yet in Israel it is as the verse says, “Make a path for Him who rides through the heavens; Yah is His name,” and, “Trust in God forever, for in Yah, God, is the Rock of worlds.” Therefore, when the blessed God’s will is clear before them, they act swiftly, without deliberation of their own. The speed of the nations, however, is only expansion without understanding. Therefore God desires neither it nor even their settled judgment.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim uses the same image of the Patriarchs running like horses and supplies a distinction that helps read Rav Tzadok’s praise of alacrity. Israel acts swiftly when the Divine will is clear; unrestrained expansion is a different kind of speed. This clarifies the direction of Abraham’s effort without converting the contrast between standing and walking into a blanket rule that haste is always preferable.

records.themeTitle: Why the soul enters the concealed world
records.themeSummary: The soul’s journey ends in this world, in a body. The descent gives its holiness a setting in which it can become evident through difficulty.
records.originHebrew: "אֶל הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר אַרְאֶךָּ" – דָּא אִיהוּ הַאי עַלְמָא, וְהַיְינוּ הַגּוּף.
records.originEnglish: “To the land that I will show you”—this is this world, namely the body.
records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 12:12
records.targetHebrew: כִּי מִצִּדּוֹ לֹא הָיָה חָפֵץ אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ לִכְנוֹס בְּהַסְתָּרַת עִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְרָצָה לִהְיוֹת תָּמִיד בִּבְהִירוּת, וּכְעִנְיַן דְּאִיתָא בְּסִטְרֵי תּוֹרָה (לֶךְ לְךָ עט עַמּוּד ב): "אַבְרָהָם – דָּא נִשְׁמְתָא", וְהַנְּשָׁמָה מִצִּדָּהּ לֹא תַחְפּוֹץ לֵירֵד לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה; אָכֵן קוֹדֶם שֶׁתִּכָּנֵס בְּתוֹךְ הַגּוּף לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֲזַי אֵין הַכָּרָה כָּל כָּךְ מַהוּ יְקָרוּתָהּ, מֵאַחַר שֶׁהִיא בֵּין הָעוֹמְדִים לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, מַלְאֲכֵי מַעְלָה הָאוֹמְרִים שִׁירָה לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ תָּמִיד, וְאֵין שָׁם שׁוּם הַסְתָּרָה כְּלָל רַק בְּהִירוּת, וְאֵין זֶה רְבוּתָא שֶׁעוֹמֶדֶת בִּקְדֻשָּׁתָהּ. אָכֵן כְּשֶׁתִּתְעָרֵב נִשְׁמַת אֱלוֹהַּ מִמַּעַל עִם גּוּשׁ עָפָר מִן הָאֲדָמָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אֲזַי מַה גָּדְלָה קְדֻשָּׁתָהּ מִקְּדֻשַּׁת צְבָאֵי מַעְלָה שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם זֶה הַכֹּחַ לִכְנוֹס בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
records.targetEnglish: For his own part, Abraham our father did not wish to enter the concealment of this world’s affairs; he wished always to remain in clarity. This resembles what is stated in Sitrei Torah: “Abraham—this is the soul.” For its own part, the soul does not wish to descend to this world. Yet before it enters the body in this world, its preciousness is not so clearly recognized. It is then among those who stand before the blessed God—the angels on high who constantly sing before Him. There is no concealment there, only clarity, so its remaining in holiness is no extraordinary distinction. But when a Divine soul from above is mingled with a clod of earthly matter in this world, how greatly its holiness exceeds that of the heavenly hosts, who do not possess this power to enter the affairs of this world.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains why the soul should leave the clarity of its upper setting at all. Holiness that persists when joined to earthly matter reveals a power not displayed among the angels who remain in uninterrupted clarity. This supplies a purpose for the descent mapped in Lech Lecha, while leaving Rav Tzadok’s distinct names for the upper levels intact.

records.themeTitle: Spiritual awakening does not end the struggle
records.themeSummary: The soul brings holiness into the body, while the evil inclination accompanies earthly life. The later awakening to service should not be mistaken for an automatic disappearance of that challenge.
records.originHebrew: וְכֵן בְּכָל אָדָם, הַנְּשָׁמָה יוֹרֶדֶת לַגּוּף בְּכָל הַקְּדוּשׁוֹת, רַק הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע הוֹלֵךְ עִמָּהּ תֵּיכֶף, כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו", וְנִדְרָשׁ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק ג דִּבְרָכוֹת הֲלָכָה ה) וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה (פָּרָשָׁה לד): "מִשָּׁעָה שֶׁהוּא נִנְעָר לָצֵאת מִמְּעֵי אִמּוֹ". וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמַר: "דְּהָא מִתְּרֵיסַר שְׁנִין וּלְעֵילָא נִשְׁמְתָא אִתְעָרַת לְמִפְלַח פּוּלְחָנָא וְכוּלֵי";
records.originEnglish: So it is with every person: the soul descends into the body with all the holy qualities, but the evil inclination accompanies it immediately, as it says, “For the inclination of the human heart is evil from his youth.” The Jerusalem Talmud and Bereishit Rabbah interpret this as “from the time he stirs to leave his mother’s womb.” Afterward [the Zohar] says: “For from twelve years onward the soul awakens to perform service,” and so forth.
records.targetHebrew: כְּפִי יִתְרוֹן הַדַּעַת וְהַחָכְמָה שֶׁבָּאָדָם, כָּךְ מִתְגַּבְּרִים לְעֻמָּתָן הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת בְּמוֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן: "יוֹסִיף דַּעַת יוֹסִיף מַכְאוֹב]" (קֹהֶלֶת א, יח). וְכֵן עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע: עַל יְדֵי שֶׁנִּכְנַס בּוֹ דַּעַת טוֹב נִכְנַס גַּם כֵּן הַהֵיפֶךְ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (סוֹטָה כא:): נִכְנְסָה חָכְמָה – נִכְנְסָה עַרְמוּמִיּוּת, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "אֲנִי חָכְמָה שָׁכַנְתִּי] עָרְמָה" (מִשְׁלֵי ח, יב). וְאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין (ע:): אֵין הַתִּינוֹק יוֹדֵעַ לִקְרוֹת "אַבָּא" וְ"אִמָּא" עַד שֶׁטּוֹעֵם דָּגָן, וְנִמְצָא אָז נִכְנַס בּוֹ דַּעַת וְחָכְמָה, וְאָז מַרְחִיקִין מִצּוֹאָתוֹ (סֻכָּה מב:), וּמְפוֹרָשׁ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת (פֶּרֶק ג הֲלָכָה ה) הַטַּעַם: שֶׁמַּחְשְׁבוֹתָיו רָעוֹת. וְכֵן שָׁמַעְתִּי, כִּי בִּשְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה שֶׁנִּכְנַס יֵצֶר טוֹב, שֶׁאָז הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע מִתְגַּבֵּר, וְכֵן אָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב.): "כָּל הַגָּדוֹל מֵחֲבֵירוֹ יִצְרוֹ גָּדוֹל הֵימֶנּוּ]".
records.targetEnglish: The greater the knowledge and wisdom in a person, the stronger the corresponding imaginings in his mind and heart, in the sense of “He who increases knowledge increases pain.” So too with the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil: when knowledge of good entered, its opposite also entered. As stated in Sotah 21b, when wisdom enters, cunning enters: “I, wisdom, dwell with cunning.” Sanhedrin 70a teaches that an infant does not know how to call “Father” and “Mother” until it tastes grain. Knowledge and wisdom then enter it, and one must then distance oneself from its excrement. The Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 3:5, explicitly gives the reason: its thoughts are bad. I likewise heard that at thirteen, when the good inclination enters, the evil inclination grows stronger. As they said, “Whoever is greater than another has a greater inclination.”
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik adds a precise qualification to the transition in Lech Lecha: at thirteen, when the good inclination enters, the opposing inclination can also intensify. Pri Tzadik’s quoted Zohar says “from twelve years onward,” while Tzidkat gives the thirteen-year formulation; these are kept distinct. The comparison concerns the relation of awakening and struggle. Increased understanding requires corresponding effort, which helps explain why Rav Tzadok places subsequent repentance after the soul’s awakening rather than treating maturity itself as complete repair.

records.themeTitle: Concealment and the work attributed to a person
records.themeSummary: The soul enters a world in which darkness precedes light. Torah and mitzvot give the person a way to work through that concealment.
records.originHebrew: וְאַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁמְּתַקֵּן הַכֹּל עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה, אוֹמֵר לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: "לְךָ טַל יַלְדֻתֶךָ", שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁעָבַר עָלָיו בִּימֵי יַלְדוּתוֹ כַּטַּל הַפּוֹרֵחַ, שֶׁמְּבָרֵר אוֹתוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִטַּלָּא דְעַתִּיקָא שֶׁכֵּן הָיָה מְסוּדָּר מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית לִהְיוֹת בְּרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא, כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הָאוֹר בִּשְׁלֵימוּת, דְּלֵית נְהוֹרָא אֶלָּא הַהוּא דְּנָפֵיק מִגּוֹ חֲשׁוֹכָא כָּאָמוּר.
records.originEnglish: Afterward, when he repairs everything through repentance, the blessed God says to him, “Yours is the dew of your youth.” Everything that passed over him in his youth is like dew that flies away. The blessed God clarifies it for him from the dew of Atika: it had been ordered from the six days of Creation that darkness should come first and light afterward, so that the light should be complete—for there is no light except that which emerges from darkness, as explained.
records.targetHebrew: ולזה ג"כ אם האדם יעמוד תמיד בבהירות כמו שמים, אז לא נחשב כלל עבודתו שביגיע כפו זכה לזה. על כן הסתיר השי"ת את דרכו, והאדם אינו עומד תמיד בבהירות כמו שמים. ולזה נתן השי"ת לעמו ישראל תורה ומצות, וע"י הסבלנות של תורה ומצות, כדאיתא בש"ס (ברכות יז.) אלופנו בתורה ומסובלים במצות, יכול האדם להזדכך ולעמוד בבהירות כמו מקודם ויהיה ע"י עבודתו, וכדאיתא (אבות פרק ו) רצה הקב"ה לזכות את ישראל לפיכך הרבה להם תורה ומצות, שעל ידי תורה ומצות יכול האדם להזדכך ולעמוד בבהירות נגד השי"ת. וזה הענין היה במתן תורה, שאז ג"כ קטרגו המלאכים ואמרו מה אדיר שמך בכל הארץ אשר תנה הודך על השמים. והיינו שאמרו מאחר שהשי"ת חפץ לזכך את הבריאה הלא ביד השי"ת לזכך את הבריאה בבת אחת שיעמדו תמיד כמו שמים, ואין צריכין כלל לתורה ומצות. וזה שהשיב להם משרע"ה, כלום יצר הרע יש ביניכם כו', אף שהם עומדים תמיד בבהירות עצום, אבל לא שייך שיהיה נקרא עבודתם על שם יגיע כפם. והרצון של השי"ת הוא כעת שעבודת ישראל יהיה ע"י תורה ומצות, ויהיה נקרא על שמם. וכמו שכתוב (תהילים ק״ה:ח׳) דבר צוה לאלף דור, ונדרש במדרש (תנחומא לך יא) על מתן תורה. שראוי היה שינתן תורה לאלף דור ומפני מה נתנה לכ"ו דור על שהיו ישרים וכו'. והיינו, כי באם היה נותנה לאלף דור היה הכל מצד השי"ת, והיה בהכרח לקים את התורה בלי שום בחירה. והשי"ת חפץ להיטיב לבריותיו ורצה לקרות העבודה על שם האדם. על כן הקדים לכ"ו דור, כדי שיהיה להם בחירה והאדם יבחר בטוב וימאס ברע, ויהיה נקרא יגיע כפו.
records.targetEnglish: If a person always stood in clarity like the heavens, his service would not be counted as something he attained through the labor of his hands. Therefore the blessed God concealed His way, and a person does not always stand in clarity like the heavens. For this reason He gave His people Israel Torah and mitzvot. Through bearing Torah and mitzvot—as the Talmud says, “Our leaders are in Torah and laden with mitzvot”—a person can become refined and stand in clarity as before, but now through his service. This is the meaning of “The Holy One, blessed be He, wished to grant merit to Israel; therefore He gave them abundant Torah and mitzvot”: through Torah and mitzvot a person can become refined and stand in clarity before the blessed God. This also occurred at the giving of the Torah. The angels again protested, “How mighty is Your name throughout the earth; place Your majesty upon the heavens.” They were saying that, since the blessed God wished to refine creation, He could refine it all at once so that it would always stand like the heavens, without any need for Torah and mitzvot. Moses answered them, “Do you have an evil inclination?” Although they always stand in tremendous clarity, their service cannot be called the labor of their hands. The blessed God’s present will is that Israel’s service should come through Torah and mitzvot and be attributed to them. As it says, “The word He commanded for a thousand generations,” which the Midrash applies to the giving of the Torah: it would have been fitting for the Torah to be given after a thousand generations, so why was it given after twenty-six generations? Because they were upright, and so forth. Had He given it after a thousand generations, everything would have come from the blessed God’s side, and Torah would have been kept of necessity, with no choice. The blessed God wished to benefit His creatures and to attribute the service to the person. He therefore brought it forward to the twenty-sixth generation, so that they would have choice: a person would choose good and reject evil, and this would be called the labor of his hands.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains why the existence of an evil inclination is relevant to the gift of Torah. God wishes the restored clarity to be reached through the person’s service and to be called the fruit of that person’s effort. This illuminates the purpose of the darkness in Lech Lecha without treating a chosen transgression as necessary or desirable: the target explicitly describes choosing good and rejecting evil.

records.themeTitle: Shabbat reveals the source that sustains every action
records.themeSummary: The meal of Atika is presented as an opportunity for retrospective repair. Shabbat’s rest makes the sustaining source of human activity more evident.
records.originHebrew: וּבְשַׁבָּת בִּסְעוּדָתָא דְעַתִּיקָא יָכוֹל הָאָדָם לִזְכּוֹת לְתַקֵּן כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כִּזְכִיּוֹת, כַּשָּׁנִים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וְכוּלֵי; וְזֶה מִקְּדֻשַּׁת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁזָּכָה לְטַלָּא דְעַתִּיקָא.
records.originEnglish: On Shabbat, at the meal of Atika, a person can merit to repair all his deeds so that they become merits, like those years that have been ordered, and so on. This comes from the holiness of Abraham our father, who attained the dew of Atika.

records.targetEnglish: Dew signifies the essential will stripped of any garment. Therefore the Talmud says that dew is not withheld: rain signifies the will clothed in a material garment from the standpoint of human perception, whereas dew has no garment at all. It is the clarity of the will as it is in its Divine source, the light of life that flows secretly into everything in the world. It is that which proceeds from God’s mouth, giving life and existence to all things. Therefore, in Isaac’s blessing, “You are mighty,” we mention “He brings down the dew.” Dew signifies this will that flows life into all things, for in truth there is no life in the world except the life flowing from this will. This too is Isaac’s quality of might: to illuminate in this world that there is judgment and a Judge—that no creature possesses any independent power, but must receive the power of life anew from the blessed God at every moment. We therefore speak of the resurrection of the dead in Isaac’s blessing. The dew with which the Holy One, blessed be He, will revive the dead is awakened through Isaac’s quality: through him, recognition is awakened in all things that all their life comes only from the Divine will flowing within them. Dew signifies that will, wholly without human action. Yet all His desire is that the flow from this dew be recognizable also in this world, within the perception of this world and in all actions. He therefore arranged for there to be weekday dew: on weekdays, the flow comes through the servant Metatron, as explained in the holy Zohar, to indicate that it is clothed and descends through an intermediary, through human action. On weekdays a person receives the flow through his actions, although his essential life always comes from what proceeds from God’s mouth, which has no garment. On weekdays, however, this light is clothed and received through various screens and garments. On Shabbat this light is explicitly recognizable: there is no active power except the blessed God alone and no other power in the world. All human activity then rests, and the light of this dew is explicitly recognizable. A person understands that he is nourished only from the very supernal light, from His simple will, with no action on his own part at all.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim distinguishes weekday dew, whose flow is clothed in human action, from Shabbat dew, when the source of life becomes explicit as human activity ceases. This gives substance to the setting Rav Tzadok chooses for repentance’s retrospective illumination. It explains why Shabbat is an apt occasion for that recognition; it does not claim that ceasing work alone performs the repentance described in the complete origin section. Rav Tzadok associates the meal here with Abraham; the target develops Isaac’s recognition and later Jacob’s dew. The connection concerns Shabbat’s disclosure of the source, without identifying these distinct patriarchal associations.

records.themeTitle: Uncommanded service and the need for a command
records.themeSummary: Abraham’s Torah grew through the wisdom God placed within him before the commandments were given. This does not make every act of personal initiative equivalent.

records.originEnglish: Abraham our father, whose quality was love, as it says, “The seed of Abraham, My beloved,” observed every fine detail of the mitzvot, including all the Sages’ detailed requirements, such as eruv tavshilin, whose purpose is to select a fine portion for Shabbat. For Abraham our father, the whole Torah had the character of Oral Torah, since he had not been commanded concerning it. Rather, the blessed God provided him with his two kidneys as two teachers, teaching him Torah and wisdom, as stated in Bereishit Rabbah 61. All Abraham’s occupations and all his actions were words of Torah. Thus the holy Zohar learns: “After these words”—these are words of Torah, for it is written, “These words God spoke,” and so on. Just as there they are words of Torah, so too here. It thereby teaches that Abraham’s entire undertaking and his war against the kings were words of Torah.

records.targetEnglish: “God said to Abraham: As for you, keep My covenant, you and your descendants after you throughout their generations.” Why did Abraham not fulfill the mitzvah of circumcision before he was commanded, when the Talmud tells us that he fulfilled even eruv tavshilin? All the mitzvot guard a person so that he walks according to “God made man upright,” without turning to one side, but following the middle path. If he becomes absorbed in one particular thing, he changes and leaves the upright path. Abraham therefore fulfilled all the mitzvot before he was commanded concerning them. Circumcision, however, involves a person repairing the blessed God’s creation, which was created with a lack. Before he was commanded, he could not, on his own initiative, alter and repair the blessed God’s creation. This would have resembled saying, God forbid, “How ugly is this vessel You made!” Therefore the blessed God showed him Ishmael’s birth. In that birth too Abraham had fulfilled God’s will, for nothing Abraham did was merely optional: all his actions accorded with God’s will. Afterward, he saw that Ishmael’s deeds were not good. From this he understood that the blessed God had deliberately established a lack for a person to repair, so that the work would be attributed to the person. He thereby understood that there was a place for the mitzvah of circumcision. He did not see this until Ishmael was thirteen years old. Immediately when he understood that there was a place for circumcision, the blessed God illuminated this for him and gave him the mitzvah in an explicit utterance: His will was that human action should become evident and that the person should eat from the labor of his hands.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach explains both Abraham’s observance before being commanded and the particular reason he awaited a command for circumcision. Ordinary mitzvot guard the upright path; altering the created body required a disclosed mandate to repair its intended lack. This qualification makes Rav Tzadok’s description of Abraham’s uncommanded Oral Torah more precise.

records.themeTitle: The spiritual discernment within Abraham’s war
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok reads Abraham’s war itself as Torah. The question becomes how the purpose of such an action is clarified.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה עִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (נְדָרִים לב עַמּוּד א): "'וַיָּרֶק אֶת חֲנִיכָיו' – שֶׁהוֹרִיקָן בַּתּוֹרָה", וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִּׁ"י: שֶׁלִּמְּדָם תּוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי. וְלִכְאוֹרָה, בַּמִּלְחָמָה הָא לֹא לִמְּדָם תּוֹרָה, וְאַדְּרַבָּה, בִּיטְּלָם מִתַּלְמוּד תּוֹרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא מִקּוֹדֶם שֶׁנֶּעֱנַשׁ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁעָשָׂה אַנְגַּרְיָא בְּתַלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים; וְהָרַ"ן זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה בְּפֵירוּשׁ לָשׁוֹן אַחֵר: שֶׁהוֹרִיקָן מֵהַתּוֹרָה שֶׁעָשָׂה בָּהֶם אַנְגַּרְיָא. אַךְ פֵּירוּשׁ רַשִּׁ"י שֶׁלִּמְּדָם תּוֹרָה יֵשׁ לְהָבִין. אַךְ הַמְּכֻוָּון שֶׁזֵּירְזָן בְּמַה שֶּׁלִּמְּדָם שֶׁכָּל עֵסֶק מִלְחַמְתּוֹ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְכָאָמוּר שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשֵׂי הָאָבוֹת הָיוּ רַק דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁלָּמַד בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ מִגְּזֵירָה שָׁוָה מִפָּסוּק "אֵת הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה וְגוֹמֵר", דִּכְתִיב בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה אַחַר דִּבְּרוֹת שְׁנִיּוֹת, וְלֹא לָמַד מִדִּכְתִיב בְּדִבְּרוֹת רִאשׁוֹנוֹת "וַיְדַבֵּר אֱלֹהִים אֵת כָּל הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה".
records.originEnglish: This is the meaning of the Talmud’s statement in Nedarim 32a: “He drew out his trained men”—he drew them into Torah. Rashi explains that he taught them Torah. At first sight, however, he did not teach them Torah during the war; on the contrary, he interrupted their Torah study, as the Talmud previously says that he was punished for pressing Torah scholars into service. The Ran gives another explanation: he emptied them of Torah by pressing them into service. Rashi’s explanation that he taught them Torah therefore requires understanding. The intention is that he urged them on by teaching them that his entire undertaking in the war was words of Torah. As explained, all the Patriarchs’ actions were words of Torah. The holy Zohar derives this by a verbal analogy from “These words,” written at the giving of the Torah after the second Decalogue, rather than from “God spoke all these words” in the first Decalogue.

records.targetEnglish: “I have raised my hand to God,” and so forth. Why did Abraham our father refuse to benefit from the king of Sodom, although we find that he accepted gifts from Pharaoh and Abimelech? His undertaking to rescue Lot required clarification. Lot contained a good power, since Naamah the Ammonite and Ruth the Moabite would descend from him; the rest was evil, since Ammon and Moab descended from him, as explained. Abraham had to clarify within himself that, in its depth, his entire intention was only to rescue those two good offshoots. Wherever a person requires clarification, the counsel is first to remove all personal interests in his own benefit. Then the blessed God will clarify that even what he did contrary to the rule was also good, for “It is a time to act for God; they have annulled Your Torah.”
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach examines this same rescue of Lot and makes its spiritual work concrete: Abraham had to clarify that his deepest purpose was to rescue the good destined to emerge from Lot, and he first removed his own material interest. This illuminates how the war can itself carry Torah’s work of discernment. The target describes an exceptional clarification reached after the removal of self-interest; it does not make a desired private outcome a standing authorization to override Torah.

records.themeTitle: Oral Torah after the broken tablets
records.themeSummary: The second tablets provide the setting for halakhah, midrash, and aggadah. The Torah of repair includes a continuing development through human understanding.
records.originHebrew: אַךְ הָעִנְיָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ, שֶׁכָּל הַתּוֹרָה הָיְתָה אֵצֶל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּגֶדֶר תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה כֵּיוָן שֶׁלֹּא נִצְטַוָּה; וְאִיתָא בִּמְדְרַשׁ רַבָּה (תִּשָּׂא פָּרָשָׁה מו וּפָרָשָׁה מז): "אַל תִּצְטַעֵר שֶׁבַּלּוּחוֹת הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת לֹא הָיוּ אֶלָּא עֲשֶׂרֶת הַדִּבְּרוֹת בִּלְבַד, וּבַלּוּחוֹת שְׁנִיּוֹת אֲנִי נוֹתֵן לְךָ שֶׁיְּהֵא בָּהֶן הֲלָכוֹת, מִדְרָשׁ וְאַגָּדוֹת", עַיֵּין שָׁם. וְזֶה שֶׁלָּמַד בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ הַגְּזֵירָה שָׁוָה מֵ"הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה" דִּכְתִיב אַחַר דִּבְּרוֹת שְׁנִיּוֹת, שֶׁנִּכְלַל בָּהֶן תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה; וְכֵן כָּל עִנְיְנֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּמִלְחַמְתּוֹ הָיוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וְהַיְינוּ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה.
records.originEnglish: The matter is as we said: for Abraham our father, the entire Torah had the character of Oral Torah, since he had not been commanded. The Midrash Rabbah, Ki Tissa 46–47, teaches: “Do not grieve: the first tablets contained only the Ten Commandments, but in the second tablets I give you halakhot, midrash, and aggadot.” See there. Therefore the holy Zohar derives the verbal analogy from “These words” written after the second Decalogue, which included Oral Torah. So too, all Abraham’s undertakings and his war were words of Torah—namely, Oral Torah.

records.targetEnglish: On Yom Kippur the later tablets were given. They are the repair after the damage and the departure from the ordered course; from there Oral Torah draws its nourishment. As is known, “Remember” belongs to the masculine, and “Guard” to the feminine, and the second tablets belong to the feminine mystery. In the future, when all Oral Torah reaches completion, it too will become Written Torah: these are the later tablets. Written Torah corresponds to the first tablets, which for now are the broken tablets resting in the Ark. Then, when “He swallows up death forever,” the first tablets too will return to their former state, as stated in the Tikkunim: death is the mystery of the breaking of the tablets. “The light of the moon will be like the light of the sun”—the tablets of Written Torah—and “the light of the sun will be sevenfold, like the light of the seven days,” by which a person could see from one end of the world to the other. This is the light of the first tablets, through which there was freedom from the angel of death and the evil inclination, as in the future, when there will no longer be any separating barrier that conceals the light.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz identifies the second tablets as the source from which Oral Torah draws nourishment after the disruption of the first order. It also places that development within the eventual restoration of the first light. This gives a larger structure to Rav Tzadok’s choice of the second Decalogue as the model for Abraham’s Oral Torah, without treating the first tablets as discarded or superseded.

records.targetEnglish: So too with the first tablets, in which the blessed God showed Israel exceptional affection, as we explained elsewhere concerning the difference between the first and later tablets. The holy Zohar explains that additional letters vav appear in the second Decalogue, indicating that the disclosure was less direct. Following the first tablets, Israel’s heart had become elevated beyond its bounds, and they made the calf, as explained in Ki Tissa. This is what the Ari’s Likkutei Torah says: the first tablets were from the foundation of Imma, signifying the exceptional love called “your mother’s Torah”; therefore they were broken. The second tablets came from the light of Abba, from the mystery of awe, through measured stages, restfulness, and proper conduct, called “your father’s discipline.” Because their great inward love was surrounded by a garment of awe, they endured.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains a further difference between the tablets: the first disclosure of love exceeded the recipients’ ability to bear it, while the second clothed inner love in awe, measured development, and composure. This complements Rav Tzadok’s account of the added Oral Torah by explaining how the later revelation can endure. The two texts offer related accounts of repair, rather than identical mappings of the Divine names.

records.themeTitle: The first utterance and the knowledge given at Sinai
records.themeSummary: At Sinai, “I am the Lord your God” implanted a knowledge that embraced Torah’s particulars. The exceptional disclosure must be distinguished from the permanent obligation shared by every person.
records.originHebrew: אֲבָל יוּבַן עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה יִשָּׁקֵנִי): בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁשָּׁמְעוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל "אָנֹכִי ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ" נִתְקַע תַּלְמוּד תּוֹרָה בְּלִבָּם וְכוּלֵי, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאָז נִתְקַע תַּלְמוּד תּוֹרָה בְּלִבָּם שֶׁיָּדְעוּ מִמַּאֲמַר "אָנֹכִי" אַף הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד, דִּכְתִיב: "וְלֹא יְלַמְּדוּ עוֹד אִישׁ אֶת רֵעֵהוּ וְגוֹמֵר כִּי כוּלָּם יֵדְעוּ אוֹתִי וְגוֹמֵר". וּבְדִבּוּר "אָנֹכִי" כָּל הַתּוֹרָה, דְּכָל תַּרְיַ"ג מִצְווֹת נִקְרָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ב, פב עַמּוּד ב) "תַּרְיַ"ג עֵיטִין", וְהַיְינוּ עֵצוֹת שֶׁיִּכָּנֵס מַאֲמַר "אָנֹכִי" וְיָאִיר בַּלֵּב.
records.originEnglish: This can be understood from the Midrash in Shir HaShirim Rabbah: when Israel heard “I am the Lord your God,” Torah learning was fixed within their hearts. At that moment, Torah learning was implanted in their hearts so that from the utterance “I am” they knew even Oral Torah. This resembles the future, of which it says, “They will no longer teach each one his fellow,” for “they will all know Me.” The utterance “I am” contains the whole Torah. records.targetEnglish: Rather, when the Torah was given and they heard “I am” and “You shall have no other” directly from the Almighty, they reached the level of prophecy. Certainly at that moment alone they attained knowledge in particulars, in all the mysteries of the Divine chariot revealed to prophets, each according to his level. Therefore it says, “The Lord your God,” in the singular. But the command established for the generations in this mitzvah of “I am”—which does not say “today” and is entrusted to everyone—is knowledge in the general sense. This is the principal purpose of this command.
records.explanation: Sefer HaZikhronot carefully distinguishes the moment of Sinai from the command as it remains for later generations. The hearers then reached prophetic knowledge of particulars according to their level; the enduring command of Anokhi requires the general recognition available to everyone. This clarifies why Lech Lecha can describe an immediate, comprehensive knowledge at Sinai and still speak afterward of the labor needed to recover and develop it.

records.targetHebrew: הנה זאת המצוה, הוא המצוה האחרונה מן התרי"ג מצות. והתרי"ג מצות נקראים בזוה"ק (יתרו פ"ב:) תרי"ג עיטין דאורייתא. ואמר בזה כבוד אאמו"ר זללה"ה שלאיזה ענין הם עצות כי אין שייך לומר שהם עצות לאהבת ד' הלא אהבת ד' הוא ג"כ מצוה אחת מן התרי"ג מצות. וכן יראת ד' הוא ג"כ מצוה אחת מן התרי"ג מצות. ורק הם עצות לאדם להיות הגוף נמשך אחר רצון השי"ת, שלא יהיה לאדם שום נטיה בלב ח"ו להיפך מן רצונו של השי"ת. וכל העצות הוא הכל לבוא אל האור, כמו שהיה בעת מתן תורה. כי במתן תורה אז נקבע כל הדברות אצל כל אחד מישראל, שלא היה לאדם שום נטיה בלב היפך מרצונו ית'. ובעת שהשי"ת אמר המאמר אנכי ד' אלהיך, אז נקבע אצל כל אחד אחדות השי"ת, עד שלא היה שייך לומר המאמר לא יהיה לך. וכדאיתא בש"ס (שבת פ"ח:) שכל דיבור ודיבור שיצא מפי הקב"ה נתמלא כל העולם כולו בשמים. ופריך הגמ' כיון שמדיבור הראשון נתמלא כל העולם כולו בשמים, דיבור שני להיכן הלך, ומתרץ הגמ' העביר ראשון ראשון. היינו המאמר לא יהיה לך. ובעת שהשי"ת אמר לא יהיה לך, אז נקבע זה המאמר בלב כל אחד ואחד מישראל. וכן בכל מאמר ומאמר עד הגמר, שאמר להם השי"ת שובו לכם לאהליכם ונעלם מהם זה האור. ולהיכן נגנז זה האור בדברי תורה, היינו שאם אדם מקיים התרי"ג מצות בשלימות, אז יש לו זה האור כמו שהיה אז במעמד הר סיני, ונקבע אצלו שלא יהיה לו שום נטיה בלב היפך מרצון השי"ת. ולזה הכא במצוה האחרונה מן התרי"ג מצות כתיב כי לא תשכח מפי זרעו, והיינו כי באמת בעומק הלב, שם אין לישראל ח"ו שום נטיה מרצון השי"ת, ורק על הלבוש נעלם זה האור. ולאחר שמקיים כל המצות בשלימות, אז גם על הלבוש לא יהיה לאדם שום נטיה היפך מרצון השי"ת:
records.targetEnglish: This mitzvah [writing the Torah] is the last of the 613 mitzvot. The holy Zohar calls the 613 mitzvot “the 613 counsels of Torah.” My revered father, of blessed memory, asked: counsels toward what? They cannot simply be counsels toward love of God, since love of God is itself one of the 613 mitzvot; awe of God is likewise one of them. Rather, they are counsels by which a person’s body follows the blessed God’s will, so that there should be no inclination in the heart contrary to His will. All the counsels lead to the light as it was at the giving of the Torah. Then every utterance was fixed within each person of Israel, leaving no inclination in the heart contrary to His will. When the blessed God said, “I am the Lord your God,” Divine unity was fixed within each person so fully that there was no place for the utterance “You shall have no other.” As the Talmud says, each utterance filled the entire world with fragrant spices. It asks: if the first utterance filled the world with fragrance, where did the second go? It answers that He removed each preceding fragrance. This corresponds to “You shall have no other.” When the blessed God spoke that utterance, it was fixed in every Israelite heart, and so with each utterance, until the conclusion, when He said, “Return to your tents,” and this light became concealed from them. Where was it hidden? In words of Torah. If a person fulfills the 613 mitzvot completely, he possesses this light as it was at Sinai: it becomes fixed within him that he should have no inclination in his heart contrary to the blessed God’s will. Therefore, concerning the last mitzvah, it says, “It will not be forgotten from the mouth of his descendants.” In the depth of the heart, Israel has no inclination away from His will; the light is concealed only in the garment. After a person fulfills all the mitzvot completely, even in that garment he will have no inclination contrary to the blessed God’s will.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains what the word “counsels” accomplishes here. Since love and awe are themselves among the mitzvot, the entire set aims more broadly at bringing the body and its inclinations into harmony with God’s will. He traces this work to the light implanted at Sinai and subsequently concealed. This directly develops Rav Tzadok’s brief statement that the counsels make Anokhi shine in the heart.

records.themeTitle: Human labor draws the same original holiness
records.themeSummary: The Torah received after the failure demands expanded human wisdom, yet it remains rooted in the original Divine speech.
records.originHebrew: וּבְדִבְּרוֹת שְׁנִיּוֹת שֶׁהָיָה אַחַר הַקִּלְקוּל, וְהוּצְרְכוּ לְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה "הַרְבֵּה חָכְמָה" לְתַקֵּן "הַרְבֵּה כָּעַס", כְּתִיב: "אֶת הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה דִּבֶּר ה' וְגוֹמֵר", לְהוֹרוֹת שֶׁאַף שֶׁנִּיתַּן לָהֶם הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, מִדְרָשׁ, הֲלָכוֹת וְאַגָּדוֹת, הַרְבֵּה חָכְמָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַכֹּל הוּא מִשֵּׁם הֲוָיָ"ה, שֶׁהַכֹּל הוּא כָּלוּל בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, וְהֵם "דְּבָרַי אֲשֶׁר שַׂמְתִּי בְּפִיךָ".
records.originEnglish: In the second Decalogue, which came after the damage, they needed Oral Torah—“much wisdom” to repair “much anger.” It therefore says, “These words the Lord spoke,” indicating that, although they were given Oral Torah, midrash, halakhot, and aggadot—much wisdom—everything nonetheless comes from the name Havayah. Everything is included in Written Torah; these are “My words that I have placed in your mouth.”
records.targetHebrew: רק אחר שנשתברו הלוחות הראשונים והיה נראה לישראל שנסתלק זאת הקדושה עלאה מאתם ואבדו אותה לגמרי ח"ו לזה ע"י גודל צעקתם וחוזק עבודתם החזיר השי"ת לישראל בהלוחות האחרונות אותה קדושה בעצמה של לוחות הראשונים ולזה נקרא יום שנתנו בו לוחות האחרונות יום טוב שהוא מקרא קדש דזמינין מקדש עלאה שהוא עצמית הקדושה של הלוחות הראשונים שהוא קבוע וקיימא מצדו ית' כקדושת שבת שמתפשטת ע"י עבודת ישראל בתוך החגים והזמנים כך התפשט ע"י עבודת ישראל הקדושה עלאה מהלוחות הראשונים אל הלוחות האחרונים וכדאיתא בזוה"ק (תצא רע"ו.) על הפסוק כי הוציא שם רע על בתולת ישראל וגו' מאן דאפיק שום ביש עלה דיימא דהא ההוא אורייתא לאו איהי דא דהא לוחין דילה אתברו קב"ה יימא ליה וכו' ופרשו השמלה ואתפתחת יריעה מספר תורה ויחזון דאתמר בה פסל לך שני לוחות אבנים כראשונים וכתבתי על הלוחות את הדברים אשר היו על הלוחות הראשונים אשר שברת וכו' היינו שמעיד השי"ת על הלוחות הראשונים שלא נסתלקו מעולם ח"ו מישראל ולא נפגם ח"ו מעולם הארת קדושתם אפילו אחר שנשתברו כי הלוחות הראשונים המה כדכתיב בתולה ואיש לא ידעה ומי שהוציא שום ביש עליהם שאין עכשיו גבי ישראל אותה הקדושה של הלוחות הראשונים עליו נאמר כי הוציא שם רע על בתולת ישראל אלא שכל אותו עצמית הקדושה של הלוחות הראשונים נתלבשו בהלוחות האחרונים:
records.targetEnglish: Only after the first tablets were broken, when it appeared to Israel that this supernal holiness had departed from them and that they had lost it completely, God forbid, did the blessed God restore to Israel, through the later tablets and through the greatness of their outcry and the strength of their service, that very same holiness of the first tablets. Therefore the day on which the later tablets were given is called a festival—a sacred convocation, summoned from the supernal holiness. This is the essential holiness of the first tablets, which is fixed and enduring from His side, like the holiness of Shabbat that spreads through Israel’s service into the festivals and their appointed times. In the same way, through Israel’s service, the supernal holiness of the first tablets spread into the later tablets. Thus the Zohar explains the verse, “For he has brought a bad name upon a virgin of Israel”: one who brings a bad name upon her by saying that the former Torah is not this Torah because its tablets were broken will be answered by the Holy One, blessed be He. “They shall spread out the garment”: a scroll of the Torah will be opened, and they will see written in it, “Carve for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and I will write upon the tablets the words that were upon the first tablets which you broke.” The blessed God thereby testifies that the first tablets never departed from Israel, God forbid, and the illumination of their holiness was never damaged, even after they were broken. The first tablets are like “a virgin whom no man has known.” Of one who falsely says that Israel no longer possesses that holiness, it says, “He has brought a bad name upon a virgin of Israel.” Rather, all the essential holiness of the first tablets was clothed within the later tablets.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim distinguishes a holiness given directly from the same holiness drawn into life through Israel’s intense prayer and service. The second tablets clothe the original light rather than introducing a disconnected substitute. This directly illuminates why Rav Tzadok attributes the later Oral Torah, despite its human labor, to the Divine name and the words God places in the mouth.

records.themeTitle: The fourth blessing as the settled goal of the journey
records.themeSummary: The three patriarchal qualities culminate in a fourth support, identified with the Land of Israel. It represents the enduring realization toward which the earlier movement tends.
records.originHebrew: וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ אִיתָא: "'וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל' – בְּגִין דִּכְתִיב 'לֶךְ לְךָ'; 'וַאֲבָרֶכְךָ' – בְּגִין דִּכְתִיב 'מֵאַרְצְךָ'; 'וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ' – בְּגִין דִּכְתִיב 'וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ'; 'וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה' – בְּגִין דִּכְתִיב 'וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ'. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אָמַר: 'וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל' – מִסִּטְרָא דִימִינָא; 'וַאֲבָרֶכְךָ' – מִסִּטְרָא דִשְׂמָאלָא; 'וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ' – מִסִּטְרָא דְאֶמְצָעִיתָא; 'וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה' – מִסִּטְרָא דְאַרְעָא דְיִשְׂרָאֵל. הָא הָכָא כּוּרְסַיָּא דְאַרְבַּע סַמְכִין דְּכֻלְּהוּ כְּלִילָן בֵּיהּ בְּאַבְרָהָם".
records.originEnglish: The holy Zohar teaches: “I will make you a great nation”—because it says, “Go for yourself”; “I will bless you”—because it says, “from your land”; “I will make your name great”—because it says, “from your birthplace”; “You shall be a blessing”—because it says, “from your father’s house.” Rabbi Shimon says: “I will make you a great nation”—from the right side; “I will bless you”—from the left side; “I will make your name great”—from the middle; “You shall be a blessing”—from the side of the Land of Israel. Here is a throne with four supports, all of them included within Abraham.

records.targetEnglish: “You shall be a blessing” concerns the concluding seal—that is, the ultimate purpose of recognizing the honor of Heaven, which is King David’s level, the culmination and end of creation. Therefore we also conclude with “Shield of David.” As is known, David’s kingship is itself the level of the Land of Israel. This is the place the blessed God promised him repeatedly: “I will establish a place for My people Israel”—a fixed place that will never be shaken. This is the purpose of service and the end of the journey away from those three things: to arrive “at the land that I will show you.”
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explicitly identifies the fourth blessing with David’s kingship, the Land of Israel, and a settled place that does not fall away. It presents this as the purpose of the departure from the three earlier attachments. This explains the fourth support’s place in the structure that Lech Lecha first quotes and later develops through David and the Messiah.

records.themeSummary: The Land of Israel forms the fourth support in the quoted pattern. The seal image explains a lasting imprint within the recipient.

records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה דְּאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ הַנַּ"ל: "'וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה' – מִסִּטְרָא דְּאַרְעָא דְיִשְׂרָאֵל", הוּא מִדַּת מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם, שֶׁזֶּה הוּא הַסְּגֻלָּה הַקְּבוּעָה בַּמִּדָּה הַזֹּאת; שֶׁעַל כָּל הַמִּדּוֹת נֶאֱמַר עֲלֵיהֶם (בְּהַקְדָּמַת תִּקּוּנֵי זֹהַר יז עַמּוּד ב): "כַּד אַנְתְּ תִּסְתַּלַּק מִנְּהוֹן, יִשְׁתָּאֲרוּן כְּגוּפָא בְּלָא נִשְׁמָתָא", אֲבָל בְּמִדַּת מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם אִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (מִשְׁפָּטִים קיד עַמּוּד א): "'שִׂימֵנִי כַחוֹתָם עַל לִבֶּךָ' (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ח, ו) – אָרְחָא דְּחוֹתָם, כֵּיוָן דְּאִתְדַּבַּק בְּהַהוּא אֲתַר דְּאִתְדַּבַּק בֵּיהּ, שָׁבֵיק בֵּיהּ כָּל דְּיוּקְנֵיהּ, אַף עַל גַּב דְּהַאי חוֹתָם אָזֵיל הָכָא וְהָכָא וְכוּלֵי, כָּל דְּיוּקְנֵיהּ שָׁבֵיק תַּמָּן וְתַמָּן קַיְּימָא".
records.targetEnglish: This is the meaning of the cited Zohar: “You shall be a blessing—from the side of the Land of Israel.” It is the quality of the kingdom of Heaven, whose special property is fixed within it. Concerning the other qualities, the introduction to the Tikkunei Zohar says: “When You depart from them, they remain like a body without a soul.” But concerning the kingdom of Heaven, the Zohar explains “Set me as a seal upon your heart”: the way of a seal is that, once it adheres to the place where it is pressed, it leaves its complete form there. Even though the seal itself goes here and there, it leaves its complete form in that place, and there the form remains.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains the same Zoharic phrase through the distinctive quality of the kingdom of Heaven: a seal leaves its complete form where it was pressed, even after the seal moves away. This supplies an account of endurance for the fourth support and prepares Lech Lecha’s later joining of the Land, David, and a final seal.

records.themeTitle: The wish for an enduring recognition of God
records.themeSummary: Abraham’s broad outreach is redirected toward a lasting people. The issue is whether the recognition he teaches can continue after him.
records.originHebrew: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ הָיְתָה מִדָּתוֹ חֶסֶד שֶׁהוּא עִנְיַן הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת, וְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל לְפַרְסֵם כְּבוֹד אֱלֹהוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת רַב בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם; וְלָכֵן גִּיֵּיר גֵּרִים הַרְבֵּה לְהַכְנִיס כָּל הָעוֹלָם תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַשְּׁכִינָה. וְאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: "לֶךְ לְךָ" מֵאוֹתוֹ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁבֵּין הָאוּמּוֹת, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל הַגֵּרִים שֶׁגִּיֵּיר חָזְרוּ לְסוּרָם אַחַר פְּטִירָתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּפִרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק כט, עַיֵּין שָׁם), וְהַיְינוּ הַגֵּרִים שֶׁגִּיֵּיר בְּאֶרֶץ חָרָן, כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְאֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה. וּכְנֶגֶד זֶה "וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל" – וְהַיְינוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בְּזַרְעֲךָ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה: "אוֹתָהּ אֻמָּה שֶׁכָּתוּב בָּהּ: 'כִּי מִי גוֹי גָּדוֹל', אֲנִי מַעֲמִיד מִמְּךָ".
records.originEnglish: Abraham our father’s quality was kindness, which means expansion. He sought to spread awareness of the honor of God’s divinity widely throughout the world, and therefore converted many people, seeking to bring the entire world under the wings of the Divine Presence. The Holy One, blessed be He, told him, “Go for yourself,” away from that expansion among the nations. For all the converts he had made returned to their former ways after his passing, as stated in Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 29. These were the converts he made in Haran, “the souls they had made in Haran,” as explained in Bereishit Rabbah. Corresponding to this came “I will make you a great nation”: the expansion of holiness within your seed. As Bereishit Rabbah says, “That nation of which it says, ‘For what great nation’—I shall establish it from you.”
records.targetHebrew: וּכְשֶׁרָאָה אַחַר כָּךְ דְּגַם הוּא יַחְשֹׁב: "אָנֹכִי הֶעֱשַׁרְתִּי וְגוֹמֵר" [בְּרֵאשִׁית י״ד:כ״ג], שֶׁעֲדַיִן לֹא הִשִּׂיג כְּלָל אֵיךְ הַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וַעֲדַיִן לֹא עָלָה בְּיָדוֹ כְּלוּם מִשְּׁלֵמוּת הָאֱמוּנָה, עַל זֶה נִתְיָרֵא מְאֹד, דְּרָאָה שֶׁכָּל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ לְמַגָּן; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת מִכָּל "הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן" [בְּרֵאשִׁית י״ב:ה׳] לֹא מָצִינוּ שֶׁנִּשְׁאַר אֶחָד מֵהֶם וּמִצֶּאֱצָאֵיהֶם תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַשְּׁכִינָה, וּכְמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּפִרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק כ״ט), דִּלְאַחַר מִיתַת אַבְרָהָם חָזְרוּ כֻּלָּם לְטָעוּתָם. וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר לוֹ ה': "אַל תִּירָא וְגוֹמֵר" [בְּרֵאשִׁית ט״ו:א׳]. וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, הֲגַם דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִבְטִיחוֹ: "שְׂכָרְךָ הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד" [שָׁם], וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתְךָ לֹא לְחִנָּם, אָמַר לוֹ: "מַה תִּתֶּן לִי וְאָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ עֲרִירִי" [שָׁם ט״ו:ב׳], הַיְינוּ דְּחָשַׁב תְּחִלָּה כָּל אוֹתָם הַנְּפָשׁוֹת שֶׁעָשָׂה הֵם תּוֹלְדוֹתָיו, דְּהַמְלַמֵּד בֶּן חֲבֵרוֹ תּוֹרָה כְּאִלּוּ יְלָדוֹ [סַנְהֶדְרִין י״ט עַמּוּד ב׳], וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הִתְגַּלּוּת הָאֱלֹהוּת בָּעוֹלָם אַחַר מוֹתוֹ עַל יְדֵיהֶם;
records.targetEnglish: When Abraham afterward saw that even [the king of Sodom] would think, “I made Abram rich,” he realized that the king still had not understood that everything comes from the blessed God and had attained none of the perfection of faith. Abraham became very afraid, seeing his entire effort as fruitless. Indeed, of “the souls they made in Haran,” we find that not one of them or their descendants remained under the wings of the Divine Presence. As the Sages said in Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 29, after Abraham’s death they all returned to their error. Therefore God told him, “Do not fear.” Nevertheless, although the blessed God promised him, “Your reward is very great”—your effort is not in vain—he said, “What can You give me, when I go childless?” At first he had thought that all those souls he had made were his children, since one who teaches another person’s son Torah is as though he had fathered him, and that the revelation of divinity would continue to spread in the world through them after his death.
records.explanation: Poked Akarim examines the disappointment that makes the promise of a lasting nation meaningful. Abraham wants others to recognize God for themselves; when even an apparently transformed disciple still credits human wealth, he fears that his mission will leave no enduring trace. His concern about being childless is therefore tied to the continuation of Divine recognition, clarifying the transition from converts to seed in Lech Lecha.

records.themeTitle: An unfinished mission despite earlier influence
records.themeSummary: Abraham’s existing influence does not yet complete the task of establishing an enduring continuation. The promise of seed opens a further stage of service.
records.originHebrew: וְהַיְינוּ כִּי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ הָיְתָה מִדָּתוֹ חֶסֶד שֶׁהוּא עִנְיַן הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת, וְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל לְפַרְסֵם כְּבוֹד אֱלֹהוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת רַב בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם; וְלָכֵן גִּיֵּיר גֵּרִים הַרְבֵּה לְהַכְנִיס כָּל הָעוֹלָם תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַשְּׁכִינָה. וְאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: "לֶךְ לְךָ" מֵאוֹתוֹ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁבֵּין הָאוּמּוֹת, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל הַגֵּרִים שֶׁגִּיֵּיר חָזְרוּ לְסוּרָם אַחַר פְּטִירָתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּפִרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק כט, עַיֵּין שָׁם), וְהַיְינוּ הַגֵּרִים שֶׁגִּיֵּיר בְּאֶרֶץ חָרָן, כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְאֶת הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ בְחָרָן", וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה. וּכְנֶגֶד זֶה "וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ לְגוֹי גָּדוֹל" – וְהַיְינוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בְּזַרְעֲךָ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה: "אוֹתָהּ אֻמָּה שֶׁכָּתוּב בָּהּ: 'כִּי מִי גוֹי גָּדוֹל', אֲנִי מַעֲמִיד מִמְּךָ".
records.originEnglish: Abraham our father’s quality was kindness, which means expansion. He sought to spread awareness of the honor of God’s divinity widely throughout the world, and therefore converted many people, seeking to bring the entire world under the wings of the Divine Presence. The Holy One, blessed be He, told him, “Go for yourself,” away from that expansion among the nations. For all the converts he had made returned to their former ways after his passing, as stated in Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 29. These were the converts he made in Haran, “the souls they had made in Haran,” as explained in Bereishit Rabbah. Corresponding to this came “I will make you a great nation”: the expansion of holiness within your seed. As Bereishit Rabbah says, “That nation of which it says, ‘For what great nation’—I shall establish it from you.”
records.targetHebrew: כי זאת היה אברהם יודע שצריך להיות השארה מזאת ההארה שנתגלה על ידו בעולם מי הוא בעל הבירה אך היה סבור שכבר פעל השארה בעולם ע"י הנפש אשר עשו בחרן וגם ע"י שהוליד נשמתין לגיורין ואין מהצורך עוד לו להולדה אחרת לזה אמר לו השי"ת מאי דעתך שכבר גמרת פעולת עבודתך בשלימות ואינך צריך עוד להולדה הלא כל כמה שלא פעלת בעבודתך שיהיה נשאר אחריך השארה מעצמותך בקביעות עדי עד לא גמרת עדיין כלום.
records.targetEnglish: Abraham knew that there must be an enduring continuation of the illumination revealed through him in the world: who is the Master of the palace. But he thought he had already established that continuation in the world through “the souls they made in Haran,” and through his bringing forth souls for converts, so that he no longer needed another kind of birth. Therefore the blessed God said to him: “What do you think—that you have completed the action of your service and no longer need to bring forth offspring? As long as you have not accomplished through your service that a continuation of your own essence should remain after you, fixed forever, you have not yet completed anything.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim directly distinguishes the souls Abraham brought close from a continuation of his own essence that endures permanently. Abraham had taken the earlier achievement as a completed legacy; God reveals that another stage remains. This explains the redirection of expansion in Lech Lecha while preserving the value of the previous work as a stage in the mission.

records.themeTitle: Why restriction can intensify blessing
records.themeSummary: Isaac’s restraint is paired with extraordinary blessing. Limiting where the flow goes can intensify what the fitting recipient receives.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁאוֹמְרִים "אֱלֹהֵי יִצְחָק" – מִדַּת "הַגִּבּוֹר", דִּגְבוּרָה הִיא מִדַּת צִמְצוּם. וּמְרַמֵּז בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ: "וַאֲבָרֶכְךָ – מִסִּטְרָא דִשְׂמָאלָא", שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בּוֹ בְּרָכָה מְפוֹרֶשֶׁת: "וַיִּמְצָא בַּשָּׁנָה הַהִוא מֵאָה שְׁעָרִים וַיְבָרֲכֵהוּ ה'", כִּי מִדַּת הַצִּמְצוּם שָׁם צָרִיךְ לִבְרָכָה. וְגַם לְהַמִּדְרָשׁ שֶׁהוּבָא בְּרַשִּׁ"י: "'וַאֲבָרֶכְךָ' – בְּמָמוֹן", זֶהוּ מִמִּדָּתוֹ, דִּכְתִיב: "מִצָּפוֹן זָהָב יֶאֱתֶה", וְשֶׁיַּעֲשִׁיר יַצְפִּין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא כה עַמּוּד ב); וּבְיִצְחָק נֶאֱמַר: "כִּי גָדַל מְאֹד", שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "זֶבֶל פִּרְדוֹתָיו וְלֹא כַּסְפּוֹ וּזְהָבוֹ שֶׁל אֲבִימֶלֶךְ", דְּכָל כָּךְ הָיָה עָשְׁרוֹ בְּהַפְלָגָה, כְּמַשְׁמָעוּת לְשׁוֹן "מְאֹד" דִּקְרָא.
records.originEnglish: This is what we express by saying “the God of Isaac”—the quality of “the Mighty,” for might is the quality of restriction. The holy Zohar alludes to it: “I will bless you—from the left side.” We find an explicit blessing concerning Isaac: “He found in that year a hundredfold, and the Lord blessed him,” for the quality of restriction requires blessing. The Midrash cited by Rashi, “I will bless you—with wealth,” likewise belongs to his quality: “From the north comes gold,” and one who wishes to become wealthy should turn north, as stated in Bava Batra. Of Isaac it says, “He grew very great”: they said, “The manure of his mules rather than Abimelech’s silver and gold.” His wealth was so extraordinary, as the word “very” indicates.
records.targetHebrew:
ויזרע יצחק בארץ ההוא וימצא בשנה ההוא מאה שערים ויברכהו ד' (בראשית כ״ו:י״ב).
הנה מדתו של יצחק הוא מדת הגבורה. כי מצד מדת חסדו ית' שהציב השי"ת בזה העולם נדמה שהולכת ההשפעה גם לעוברי רצונו. כעין דאיתא בש"ס (תענית ז'.) מטר לכל בין לצדיקים ובין לרשעים, ורק מצד מדת יצחק מגביל ההשפעה שתלך רק לעושי רצונו של מקום, ומחמת זאת ההגבלה, נמצא שהולכת ההשפעה לעושי רצונו בגודל תוקף. וזה כוונת חז"ל (שם ב'.) מאי גבורות גשמים אמר ר"י מפני שיורדין בגבורה והוא כנ"ל, כי מצד זאת המדה הולכת ההשפעה בזעף גדול. ומפני זה בברכת יצחק שהוא מחיה מתים נכללים כל הישועות, סומך נופלים ורופא חולים וכו'. וענין זה הגבלה של יצחק אע"ה הוא, כי באמת בעוה"ז נקרא בזוה"ק (משפטים צ"ה) מדת מלכות לית לה עיינין. כמו דאיתא בש"ס (ע"ז נ"ד:) הרי שגזל סאה חטים וזרעה בקרקע בדין הוא שלא תצמח אלא עולם כמנהגו נוהג, וזה נקרא לית לה עיינין. ובאמת מי שמעמיק במדה הזאת רואה, שגם במדה הזאת אית לה עיינין. והיינו מי שהולך בעבודה ומאמין בחי עולמים וזורע באמת מקבל המוציא פי ד' המונח בהטובה המחיה והמהוה את הטובה. ומי שהוא רק על הגוון, אינו מקבל רק הלבוש מהטובה בלי שום פנימיות. וזה הכל מי שמעמיק רואה זאת, אבל על הלבוש נדמה שזה מקבל טובה כמו זה, וזה נקרא עולם כמנהגו נוהג. וזה ענין של יצחק אע"ה שמאיר בזה העולם אית דין ואית דיין, שכל האומר הקב"ה ותרן יותרו חייו (ב"ק נ'.) ובזאת המדה מגביל ההשפעה שאפילו הלבוש מהטובה ג"כ לא יקבל רק עושי רצונו, נמצא שמצד זאת ההגבלה הולך הטובה לעושי רצונו בכח גדול. וזה ויזרע יצחק בארץ ההוא וימצא בשנה ההוא מאה שערים ומתרגם מאה בדשערוהי, והיינו שמצד מדתו מקבלין עושי רצונו ההשפעה בכח גדול:
records.targetEnglish: “Isaac sowed in that land and found in that year a hundredfold, and the Lord blessed him.” Isaac’s quality is might. From the standpoint of the kindness that the blessed God established in this world, the flow appears to reach even those who transgress His will, as the Talmud says that rain falls for everyone, righteous and wicked alike. Isaac’s quality limits the flow so that it goes only to those who perform God’s will. Because of this limitation, it reaches them with great force. This is the meaning of the Sages’ question, “What are the mighty powers of rain?”—because rain descends with might. Through this quality, the flow descends with tremendous force. Therefore Isaac’s blessing, “Who revives the dead,” includes all salvations: supporting the fallen, healing the sick, and so forth. Isaac’s limitation is this: in this world, the Zohar describes the kingdom as having no eyes. Thus the Talmud says: if someone steals a measure of wheat and sows it, by rights it should not grow, but the world follows its customary course. This is called having no eyes. In truth, one who looks deeply into this quality sees that it too has eyes. One who serves God, trusts in the Life of worlds, and sows receives what proceeds from God’s mouth within the good, giving that good life and existence. One who remains only at the surface receives only the garment of the good, without its inwardness. Whoever looks deeply sees this, although on the surface both appear to receive the same good. This is the world following its customary course. Isaac illuminates that there is judgment and a Judge; whoever says the Holy One, blessed be He, simply waives judgment forfeits his life. Through this quality he limits the flow so that even the outer garment of the good reaches only those who do His will. The good therefore comes to them with great force. This is “Isaac sowed in that land and found in that year a hundredfold,” rendered as a hundred times the estimated yield: through Isaac’s quality, those who do God’s will receive the flow with great force.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the connection between Isaac’s gevurah and the hundredfold harvest quoted in Lech Lecha. Restriction directs the flow toward those who serve God, and their reception includes the Divine life within the good. This makes the link between restraint and blessing explicit, rather than leaving wealth as an unexplained accompaniment to Isaac’s quality.

records.themeTitle: Selectivity grounded in generosity
records.themeSummary: Isaac narrows the circle of those he teaches because he seeks a lasting inward response. His restraint retains the generosity inherited from Abraham.
records.originHebrew: וּמִדַּת יִצְחָק הוּא הַצִּמְצוּם, שֶׁרָאָה שֶׁמִּכָּל גִּיּוּרֵי אָבִיו לֹא נִשְׁאַר, שֶׁחָזְרוּ לְסוּרָם, וְלָכֵן צִמְצֵם קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לְהִתְפַּשֵּׁט בֵּין עוֹבְדֵי כוֹכָבִים וּמַזָּלוֹת, וְלָכֵן לֹא כְּתִיב בְּיִצְחָק שֶׁגִּיֵּיר גֵּרִים, רַק בְּרֶמֶז חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב): "בְּאֶרֶץ מְגוּרֵי אָבִיו – מִגִּיּוּרֵי אָבִיו", כִּי מְעַט הָיוּ הַגֵּרִים שֶׁגִּיֵּיר, שֶׁלֹּא גִּיֵּיר רַק יְחִידִים שֶׁהֵבִין שֶׁלֹּא יַחְזְרוּ לְסוּרָם.
records.originEnglish: Isaac’s quality is restriction. He saw that none of his father’s converts remained, for they returned to their former ways. He therefore restricted his holiness from spreading among the idolaters. Accordingly, Scripture does not explicitly say that Isaac made converts, except in the Sages’ allusion: “In the land of his father’s sojournings”—from his father’s converts. The converts he made were few: he converted only particular people whom he understood would not return to their former ways.

records.targetEnglish: Isaac had a different spirit: whoever was not inwardly as he appeared outwardly should not enter the study hall. He was sparing in teaching everyone who came to him, admitting only one whose inwardness matched his outwardness. God forbid that one should think Isaac, the son of Abraham—who is called generous, “The generous of the peoples gathered, the people of the God of Abraham”—did this because he was truly miserly. Rather, he restricted himself from giving where the blessed God did not desire it. Isaac was born of Abraham to show that the quality of generosity was indeed present in him too, inherited from his father; all his sparing conduct was because he did not wish to give where the blessed God did not desire it.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explains the motive behind Isaac’s selective teaching: the generosity inherited from Abraham is present, but it is directed only where he recognizes the Divine will. This clarifies Rav Tzadok’s statement that Isaac admitted particular converts whose attachment would endure. It distinguishes restraint in giving from an absence of the desire to give.

records.themeTitle: Awe arises from the recognition of nearness
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok connects the Land, Divine appearance, and Isaac’s awe. The decisive recognition is that a person stands before the King.

records.originEnglish: “To the land that I will show you” also alludes to Isaac. We do not find a verse saying that God showed Abraham the land; the intention is “where I will appear to you,” for prophecy belongs to the Land of Israel. Although the Land had not yet been chosen, and the opening of the Mekhilta teaches that all lands were then fit for Divine speech and the resting of the Divine Presence—indeed, “Go for yourself” was spoken to him outside the Land—nonetheless the expression “He appeared” is used only afterward, immediately when Abraham came to Shechem in the Land of Israel. So too with awe, the fear of Isaac: when a person takes to heart that the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, stands over him and sees his actions, awe and fear immediately reach him. Isaac’s fear means seeing that one stands before the King. Thus the Talmud says, “Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, with their own eyes.” This is “that I will show you”—where I will appear to you.

records.targetEnglish: “Lest you take my son back there.” Awe comes from nearness: when one stands before the king, one fears him, as stated in the gloss at the beginning of Orach Chayim. Likewise, “with great awe” is the revelation of the Divine Presence. Love, by contrast, can be stronger at a distance, as in the familiar example of a son whose longing for his father increases when he is far away. The Land of Israel is the level of “I have set God before me always,” and “a land upon which the eyes of the Lord your God always rest.” Outside the Land, one is described as like someone who has no God—that is, not directly before his eyes, but at a distance. This is the meaning of “The air of the Land of Israel makes one wise.” The Sages use the word wise for recognition—as in, “Does the Master recognize Rav Pappa?”—since recognition comes from wisdom; the Land’s air brings forth the recognition of divinity, and recognition comes from nearness. Therefore Abraham warned against taking Isaac outside the Land, where there is no place for this awe, but rather love. This is what Shabbat 89b says: Isaac shows them the Holy One, blessed be He, with their own eyes. “They will see eye to eye,” and setting God directly before one’s eyes, are Isaac’s level. The capacity for this also comes through Isaac’s quality: might is restriction, through which God, as it were, limits the spread of His light so that even the lowliest person can apprehend it. As is known, “God is your shadow”: God’s response corresponds to a person’s level. When the person fears and restricts himself, so does God. It says “with their eyes,” as in “They will see eye to eye,” because awe purifies sight, as explained earlier. As Avodah Zarah says, the vessels of the eye depend on the heart, and awe is associated with the heart, as Yoma explains the verse, “But there is no heart.”
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah develops the same connection through the warning not to take Isaac outside the Land. Awe responds to felt nearness, while longing can intensify at a distance; the Land’s distinctive recognition therefore fits Isaac’s quality. The target further relates human restraint to a disclosure the recipient can bear, explaining how awe and Divine appearance work together.
