records.themeTitle: The enlargement of a name as the unfolding of life
records.themeSummary: A name expresses the life within a being. Making the name great therefore concerns the expansion and continuation of that life.
records.originHebrew: "וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ – בְּגִין דִּכְתִיב וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ", וְזֶה שֶׁאוֹמְרִים "אֱלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב", כִּי "וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ" מְרַמֵּז עַל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם. כִּי שֵׁם כָּל דָּבָר מוֹרֶה עַל הַחַיּוּת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן: "וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִקְרָא לוֹ הָאָדָם נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה הוּא שְׁמוֹ"; וַ"אֲגַדְּלָה" לְשׁוֹן גְּדוּלָּה הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת; "וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ" – שֶׁתִּהְיֶה הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת בְּחַיּוּת בְּלֹא הֶפְסֵק. וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִצַּד אַבְרָהָם עַצְמוֹ עֲדַיִן אֵין בְּטִיחוּת עַל הַקִּיּוּם לָעַד, כִּי הָיָה גַּם פְּסֹלֶת בְּזַרְעוֹ, וְכֵן בַּגֵּרִים שֶׁגִּיֵּיר כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל; אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב הוּא "שְׂפַת אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד", וְלֹא יָצָא פְּסֹלֶת מִזַּרְעוֹ, וּמֵאִתּוֹ נִתְפַּשְּׁטָה קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד. וְכֵן הַגֵּרִים שֶׁבְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכוּנּוּ, הֵם גַּם כֵּן כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד, לִהְיוֹת בָּהֶם גַּם כֵּן כֹּחַ הַקִּיּוּם לָעַד. וְזֶהוּ גִּידּוּל הַשֵּׁם, דְּהַיְינוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַחַיִּים לִזְכּוֹת לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם, דְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא וְזוֹכִים לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם, וְזֶה מִצַּד מִדַּת "אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב", וְקַו הָאֶמְצָעִי הוּא הַמַּמְשִׁיךְ מִן הַקָּצֶה אֶל הַקָּצֶה.
records.originEnglish: “I will make your name great—because it says, from your birthplace.” This is what we express by saying “the God of Jacob,” for the promise alludes to Jacob. The name of anything indicates the life within it, as it says concerning Adam, “Whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name.” Making great means expansion: the holiness should expand in unceasing life. Expansion through Abraham alone did not yet guarantee everlasting endurance, for there was an impure element among his descendants and among his converts. Jacob, however, is “The lip of truth endures forever.” No impure element issued from his descendants, and from him Israel’s holiness spread forever. Converts who are called by the name Israel likewise become as a newly born child and possess the power of enduring forever. This is the enlargement of the name: life expands to attain eternal life. All Israel has a share in the world to come and attains eternal life. This comes from the quality of truth given to Jacob; the middle line extends from one end to the other.
records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 18:5
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶה הוּא שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ: "'וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ' – מוֹסִיף אֲנִי הֵ"א עַל שִׁמְךָ", וְהוּא כִּי עוֹד לֹא נִיתַּן לוֹ כְּלָלָא דְּבִרְכָתָא, רַק נְקֻדָּה שֶׁל חַיִּים, בִּרְכַּת "וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה", שֶׁזֶּה מוֹרֶה עַל הַנְּקֻדַּת הַחַיִּים שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נוֹתֵן בָּאָדָם מִיּוֹם הִוָּלְדוֹ, שֶׁשּׁוֹאֵב מֵרָחוֹק הַהַרְחָבוֹת וּמִתְבָּרֵךְ וּמִתְגַּדֵּל בְּכָל פַּעַם עוֹד יוֹתֵר. וְזֶה הוּא רַק נְקֻדָּה מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה עָתִיד לְהִתְגַּדֵּל שְׁמוֹ בְּתוֹסֶפֶת הֵ"א, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לוֹ (בְּרֵאשִׁית יז, ה): "וְהָיָה שִׁמְךָ אַבְרָהָם"; וְעַתָּה בָּאָה לוֹ הַבְטָחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁעָתִיד לְהַגְדִּיל שְׁמוֹ, וְעַל זֶה מוֹרֶה מַאֲמַר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ "וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ", שֶׁאָז הַנְּקֻדָּה תִּתְפַּשֵּׁט בְּעֹצֶם קְדֻשָּׁתָהּ, וְכִדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (וַיִּקְרָא יא עַמּוּד ב): "הֵ"א בַּתְרָאָה דִּבִשְׁמָא קַדִּישָׁא וְכוּלֵי, וְהַהוּא אִתְפַּשְׁטוּתָא דְּנָפֵיק מִנֵּיהּ כִּגְוָונָא דְּהַהוּא נָהָר וְכוּלֵי" (וְעַיֵּין בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ מִשְׁפָּטִים קכג עַמּוּד ב).
records.targetEnglish: This is what they expounded: “I will make your name great”—I will add a heh to your name. For the full encompassing blessing had not yet been given to him, but only a point of life, the blessing “You shall be a blessing.” This signifies the point of life that the blessed God gives a person from the day of his birth, which draws expansions from afar and is blessed and grows more each time. It was only a point of the greatness his name would later attain through the addition of heh, when he was told, “Your name shall be Abraham.” Now the blessed God’s promise came that He would later make his name great. “I will make your name great” indicates that this point would then spread in its own holiness. As the Zohar says, “The last heh of the holy name,” and “the expansion that issues from it, like that river,” and so forth.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov develops the same promise by distinguishing an initial point of life from its later expansion in its own holiness. This supplies an account of how the enlargement of a name can mean an enlargement of life. His immediate discussion concerns Abraham’s added letter; Rav Tzadok associates the enduring reach of the promise with Jacob’s truth. Those distinct applications are preserved.

records.themeTitle: Jacob’s life already participates in the world to come
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok connects Jacob’s freedom from the evil inclination with an uninterrupted holy life. Mei HaShiloach explains the kind of continuity meant by “Jacob did not die.”
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וַאֲגַדְּלָה שְׁמֶךָ – בְּגִין דִּכְתִיב וּמִמּוֹלַדְתְּךָ", וְהַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב: "וּבְחֵטְא יֶחֱמַתְנִי אִמִּי", וּמִצַּד זֶה בָּא הַפְסָקַת הַחַיִּים בָּעוֹלָם; וְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהָיָה כְּמוֹ אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַקִּלְקוּל (כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים), וְלֹא הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוּם צַד שְׁלִיטָה מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וּלְכָךְ: "יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ לֹא מֵת", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תַּעֲנִית ה עַמּוּד ב); וְהוּא הַחַיּוּת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם, וְהַיְינוּ חַיּוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה שֶׁבְּזֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּלֹא הֶפְסֵק.
records.originEnglish: This is “I will make your name great—because it says, from your birthplace.” Scripture says, “In sin my mother conceived me,” and from this comes the interruption of life in the world. Jacob our father was like Adam before the damage, as explained many times, and no aspect of the evil inclination had power over him. Therefore “Jacob our father did not die,” as stated in Ta’anit 5b. He is the life within the world: the uninterrupted holy life in the seed of Israel.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 9
records.targetHebrew: וַיֶּאֱסוֹף רַגְלָיו אֶל הַמִּטָּה. אִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא (תַּעֲנִית הֵא עַמּוּד בֵּית) "יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ לֹא מֵת", הָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה כִּי עִנְיַן מִיתָה הוּא הִשְׁתַּנּוּת הָאָדָם מֵעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְעוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְיַעֲקֹב כָּל אוֹתָן שָׁנִים שֶׁהָיָה בְּמִצְרַיִם הִטְעִימוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ טִיפָּה חַיִּים מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא, עַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר עָלָיו לֹא מֵת כִּי לֹא נִשְׁתַּנָּה בְּמוֹתוֹ כְּלוּם, וְעַל זֶה מַסְמִיךְ תֵּיכֶף הַגְּמָרָא "כָּל הָאוֹמֵר רָחָב רָחָב מִיָּד נִקְרֵי" וּמַסִּיק שָׁם הַגְּמָרָא בְּיוֹדְעָהּ וּמַכִּירָהּ, וְלָזֶה הִיא סְמִיכוּת הַגְּמָרָא לְהַרְאוֹת כִּי כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּמְצָא בְּעִנְיְינֵי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה חֶמְדָּה שֶׁנִּשְׁאָר קָבוּעַ בְּלֵב הָאָדָם, כֵּן הָיָה הַטִּיפָּה חַיִּים שֶׁנִּקְבַּע בְּלֵב יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ בְּעֵת אֲשֶׁר נָטַף בּוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נִשְׁאַר בּוֹ קָבוּעַ גַּם אַחַר כָּךְ, עַל כֵּן לֹא יִתָּכֵן לְהֵאָמֵר בּוֹ לְשׁוֹן מִיתָה רַק כְּאָדָם שֶׁפּוֹשֵׁט מַלְבּוּשָׁיו וְלוֹבֵשׁ בְּגָדִים אֲחֵרִים
records.targetEnglish: “He gathered his feet into the bed.” The Talmud says, “Jacob our father did not die.” Death means a person’s change from this world to the world to come. During all the years Jacob spent in Egypt, the blessed God gave him a taste of a drop of life resembling the world to come. Therefore it is said that he did not die: nothing changed for him in his death. The Talmud immediately places beside this the statement, “Whoever says Rahab, Rahab immediately has a seminal emission,” and concludes that this applies to someone who knows and recognizes her. The juxtaposition shows that, just as there can be a worldly desire fixed permanently in the heart, so the drop of life that the blessed God caused to drip into Jacob’s heart remained fixed there afterward. Therefore the expression death does not fit him; it is like a person removing his clothes and putting on other garments.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach interprets death as a transition in the person’s mode of life. Jacob had already received a taste of the world to come during his years in Egypt, and that life remained fixed within him. This clarifies the continuity invoked in Lech Lecha and gives content to its connection between the removal of the inclination’s rule and unbroken holy vitality.

records.themeTitle: A residual root of lack and the bringing forth of holiness
records.themeSummary: The reference to Jesse concerns the serpent’s inherited residue, despite personal righteousness. Rav Tzadok distinguishes this remaining root from the final repair associated with the Messiah.
records.originHebrew: וְהוּא נֶגֶד מַה דִּכְתִיב: "וּמִבֵּית אָבִיךָ", וְהַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב: "הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי", וְאָמְרוּ (מִדְרַשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ): "אֲפִילּוּ אִם יִהְיֶה חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ צַד אֶחָד מֵעָוֹן וְכוּלֵי", וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵינוֹ נָקִי מֵהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ, וְזֶה מִצַּד עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, דְּאִיתָא (שַׁבָּת נה עַמּוּד ב): "יִשַׁי אֲבִי דָוִד דִּמְפָרֵשׁ בֵּיהּ קְרָא שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ", וְעָלָיו נֶאֱמַר "הֵן בְּעָווֹן" מָלֵא (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב שָׁם); וּמָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד יְתַקֵּן גַּם עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, וְיַמְשִׁיךְ הַחַיִּים הָאֲמִיתִּיִּים בָּעוֹלָם, כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לּוֹ וְגוֹמֵר", וְהוּא יִהְיֶה הַסּוֹף שֶׁיְּתַקֵּן הַכֹּל בָּעוֹלָם, וְיִהְיֶה "בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח".
records.originEnglish: This corresponds to “from your father’s house,” for it says, “Indeed, in iniquity I was formed.” The Midrash teaches: even the most pious of the pious cannot be without one aspect of iniquity—that is, he is not entirely free of his own enjoyment. This comes from the serpent’s counsel. Shabbat 55b says that Scripture explicitly identifies Jesse, David’s father, as having died through the serpent’s counsel. Concerning him, the Midrash expounds “in iniquity” as a full spelling. The Messiah son of David will repair even the serpent’s counsel and draw true life into the world, as it says, “He asked You for life; You gave it to him.” He will be the final culmination that repairs everything in the world, and “He will swallow up death forever.”
records.targetHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל זֶה (נִדָּה ט.): "מִי יִתֵּן טָהוֹר מִטָּמֵא? לֹא אֶחָד" (אִיּוֹב יד, ד) – יְחִידוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם; דְּלוּלֵא הַיִּחוּד הַגָּמוּר אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהָבִין זֶה, כִּי בְּתַאֲוָה זוֹ הוּא מְקוֹר הַחֶסְרוֹנוֹת שֶׁמִּן הַנָּחָשׁ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת תַּזְרִיעַ יד, ה): בֶּעָווֹן מָלֵא וְכוּלֵי, וְהוּא יִשַׁי שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה יח): "הַנָּחָשׁ הִשִּׁיאַנִי" – רָאָה אוֹתָן עֲסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי, וְאַחַר כָּךְ נוֹלַד לָהֶם הַבּוּשָׁה בָּזוֹ וְיָדְעוּ כִּי עֵירֻמִּם, דִּלְמִצְוָה אֵין בּוּשָׁה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּיַעֲקֹב דְּלֹא מֵת, שֶׁהוּא תִּיקֵּן זֶה].
records.targetEnglish: As the Sages said concerning this: “Who can bring a pure one from an impure one? Is it not the One?”—the One of the world. Without complete unity, this could not be understood. For this desire is the source of the deficiencies that come from the serpent, as the Midrash at the beginning of Tazria expounds the full spelling of “in iniquity.” This concerns Jesse, who died through the serpent’s counsel. As Bereishit Rabbah says concerning “The serpent beguiled me”: he saw them engaged [in intercourse], and afterward shame in this arose for them, and they knew that they were naked. For there is no shame in a mitzvah, as explained concerning Jacob, who did not die, for he repaired this.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik discusses Jesse and the same verse about conception, explaining why holiness can nevertheless emerge from a place bearing the serpent’s residue. Bringing the pure from the impure depends on the Divine unity, and Jacob exemplifies repair of that source. This helps distinguish the root still discussed in Lech Lecha from a claim that the person lacks all holiness or has committed a particular personal sin.

records.themeTitle: Resurrection repairs the life that passed through concealment
records.themeSummary: The final defeat of death is the completion of repair. It restores the person whose life and service passed through real suffering and concealment.
records.originHebrew: וּמָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד יְתַקֵּן גַּם עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, וְיַמְשִׁיךְ הַחַיִּים הָאֲמִיתִּיִּים בָּעוֹלָם, כְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לּוֹ וְגוֹמֵר", וְהוּא יִהְיֶה הַסּוֹף שֶׁיְּתַקֵּן הַכֹּל בָּעוֹלָם, וְיִהְיֶה "בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח".
records.originEnglish: The Messiah son of David will repair even the serpent’s counsel and draw true life into the world, as it says, “He asked You for life; You gave it to him.” He will be the final culmination that repairs everything in the world, and “He will swallow up death forever.”
records.targetHebrew: היינו כמו שאיתא בש"ס (סנהדרין צא.) הא כיצד עומדין במומן ומתרפאין, היינו שהאדם יכיר את עצמו שמאותן הסבלנות שסבל בעוה"ז יש לו עתה כח התחיה. וזה כוונתן שיעמדו במומן היינו שיכירו שמהחסרון שהיה להם בעוה"ז, שבעומק הציב השי"ת זאת שיתראה חסרון למען צדקו, בכדי שיהיה מקום לאדם להתגדר בו. ובעוה"ז סבל האדם מזה מאד, ובירר את עצמו עד מקום שידו מגעת, מזה יש לו עתה רפואה למחץ מכתו, וכמו שכתיב (זכריה ח׳:ד׳) ואיש משענתו בידו. מכאן תשובה לאומרים אין תחית המתים מן התורה. הענין כמו שביאר בזה כבוד אזמו"ר הגה"ק זללה"ה שתורה הוא כמו שאיתא בזוה"ק (מצורע נג:) אמאי אקרי תורה דאורי וגלי מה דהוה סתים דלא אתידע. וזה הוא כוונתם שהתורה מחיה את המתים, היינו שבזה המקום עצמו שנדמה לאדם קודם זה שהיה ח"ו העדר ולא הכיר מצידו כלל שנמצא גם בזה המקום אור, ושהיה גם אז מקושר בהשי"ת, יאיר לו השי"ת שבאמת בזה המקום עצמו היה מלא אור בלי הפסק רגע, ומעולם לא היה שום העדר, ורק מצד תפיסת האדם שהציב השי"ת בעוה"ז נדמה לו שנמצא העדר והסתר ח"ו, וכל דמיון ההעדר ומיתה והעתק מהשי"ת היה רק מצד תפיסת האדם. וזה הפירוש שיעמדו במומן, היינו שלעתיד יברר להם השי"ת כל זאת, כי לעתיד שיתקיים הכתוב (ישעיהו כ״ה:ח׳) בלע המות לנצח, אז יתברר שלא היה מעולם שום העדר והסתר בישראל, ומחה ד' אלהים דמעה מעל כל פנים. וזה פירוש מכאן תשובה לאומרים אין תחית המתים מן התורה, היינו שמן התורה יכיר האדם שהוא הוא בעצמו שהיה קודם התחיה, וכן הוא בעצמו גם עתה אחר התחיה:
records.targetEnglish: This is like the Talmud’s teaching in Sanhedrin: they rise with their defects and are healed. A person will recognize himself: from the sufferings he bore in this world, he now has the power of resurrection. This is the meaning of rising with their defects. They recognize that the lack they experienced in this world was, in its depth, established by the blessed God so that there would appear to be a lack for the sake of His righteousness, giving a person room to accomplish something. In this world the person suffered greatly from it and clarified himself as far as his power could reach. From this he now has healing for the wound of his affliction, as it says, “Each man with his staff in his hand.” “From here is an answer to those who say that resurrection is not taught in the Torah.” My revered grandfather explained that Torah means, as the Zohar says, that which teaches and reveals what was concealed and unknown. This is the meaning of Torah reviving the dead. In the very place where a person previously thought there was absence, and did not recognize that light was present there and that he was then connected to the blessed God, God will illuminate for him that the place itself was full of light without a moment’s interruption. There was never any absence; only from the human perception that God established in this world did absence and concealment seem to exist. All the apparent absence, death, and separation from the blessed God arose from that human perception. Thus they rise with their defects: in the future the blessed God will clarify all this for them. When “He swallows up death forever,” it will become clear that there had never been absence or concealment in Israel, and God will wipe tears from every face. This is the answer to those who say resurrection is not taught in Torah: through Torah a person will recognize that he is the very same person who existed before the resurrection, and that he himself exists now after the resurrection.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the future repair through the teaching that the dead rise with their defects and are then healed. They recognize themselves and the relation of their former struggle to their present life; Torah reveals the Divine connection that was concealed. This gives a concrete account of the final repair named in Lech Lecha, rather than treating resurrection as the arrival of an unrelated new person.

records.themeTitle: David’s final seal is contained in Abraham’s beginning
records.themeSummary: The blessings conclude with Abraham and with David. Their beginning and culmination are joined through the recognition of God’s kingship and protection.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא: "יָכוֹל יְהוּ חוֹתְמִין בְּכוּלָּם? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: 'וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה' – בְּךָ חוֹתְמִין וְכוּלֵי", כִּי עִנְיַן "מָגֵן דָּוִד" גַּם כֵּן מִצַּד אַבְרָהָם, שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: "אַל תִּירָא אַבְרָם, אָנֹכִי מָגֵן לָךְ וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁהָיָה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ מִתְפַּחֵד שֶׁמָּא נִכְשַׁל בְּאֵיזֶה חֵטְא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה: "תֹּאמַר אוֹתָן אֻכְלוּסִין שֶׁהָרַגְתִּי שֶׁמָּא הָיָה בָּהֶם צַדִּיק אֶחָד וִירֵא שָׁמַיִם אֶחָד וְכוּלֵי", וְאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: אַל תִּירָא מִכָּל מִכְשׁוֹל, אָנֹכִי מָגֵן לָךְ, וּמְסַבֵּב אוֹתְךָ מִכָּל צַד שֶׁלֹּא תִּהְיֶה שְׁלִיטָה לְשׁוּם חֵטְא לִשְׁלוֹט בָּךְ. וּקְדֻשַּׁת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּמָשִׁיחַ גַּם כֵּן מִצִּדְּךָ; וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "מָגֵן דָּוִד" בַּהַפְטָרָה, מִצַּד שֶׁהוּא יִהְיֶה הַסּוֹף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג, רמ עַמּוּד ב): "סִיּוּמָא – מַלְכָּא מְשִׁיחָא"; אֲבָל עִיקַּר הַהַתְחָלָה הוּא מִצִּדְּךָ, וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ שֶׁאֵין חוֹתְמִין אֶלָּא בָּךְ.
records.originEnglish: This is what the Talmud says: “Might one conclude with all of them? The verse therefore says, ‘You shall be a blessing’—with you they conclude.” For “Shield of David” also comes from Abraham, to whom the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “Do not fear, Abram; I am a shield for you.” Abraham was afraid that he might have stumbled into sin, as Bereishit Rabbah says: “Perhaps among the hosts I killed there was one righteous person who feared Heaven.” The Holy One, blessed be He, told him: do not fear any stumbling; I am a shield for you, surrounding you on every side so that no sin can gain power over you. The holiness of David and the Messiah also comes from you. The Haftarah concludes with “Shield of David” because he will be the culmination, as the holy Zohar says, “The conclusion is the King Messiah.” But the essential beginning comes from you; therefore they conclude only with you.
records.targetHebrew: "וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה" – בְּךָ חוֹתְמִין פְּסָחִים קיז:, וְכֵן בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה. כִּי אַבְרָהָם – רֹאשׁ הַבְּרִיאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרָכוֹת טז:: "אֵין קוֹרִין אָבוֹת אֶלָּא לִשְׁלֹשָׁה", שֶׁהֵם אֲבוֹת הָעוֹלָם וְהַהַתְחָלָה מֵהַכָּרַת הָאֱלֹהוּת, וְאַבְרָהָם – אָב לְכוּלָּם, כִּי "אַב הֲמוֹן גּוֹיִם וְגוֹמֵר" בְּרֵאשִׁית יז, ה, נִכְלַל תֹּאַר "אָב" בִּשְׁמוֹ כִּי "אָב" רָצָה לוֹמַר: הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת לָעֲנָפִים, וְהוּא מִמִּדַּת הַחֶסֶד שֶׁהוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת. וְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר חֵלֶק ג, רנו עַמּוּד ב: "אַבָּא יָסַד בְּרַתָּא", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר, כִּי אַבְרָהָם, יִצְחָק, יַעֲקֹב, וְדָוִד אָב, וְאֵם, בֵּן, וּבַת; וְ"סוֹף מַעֲשֶׂה בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה", כִּי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא מָשִׁיחַ, הוּא סוֹף הַבְּרִיאָה, וּלְכָךְ בּוֹ חֲתִימַת הַבְּרָכָה מִתְיַיחֵס לְהַתְחָלַת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה. וְהַחֲתִימָה בְּ"מָגֵן", כְּמוֹ בַּמּוֹעֲדִים: הַתְחָלַת הַהַכָּרָה בְּפֶסַח – חֹדֶשׁ הָאָבִיב, בּוֹ הַתְחָלַת קַבָּלַת אֱלֹהִית; וְהַחֲתִימָה בְּחַג הָאָסִיף, שֶׁהוּא סֻכָּה "לְמַחְסֶה וּלְמִסְתּוֹר" יְשַׁעְיָה ד, ו, שֶׁהוּא הַבְּטִיחוּת שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְגִנּוֹ; וְדָבָר זֶה אַחַר הַשְׁלָמַת עֲבוֹדַת הַקַּיִץ, מַדְרֵגַת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּשֵׁם הָאֲדֹנוּת, שֶׁהוּא תְּהִלִּים טז, ח: "שִׁוִּיתִי ה' לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד" כְּאָדוֹן לְעַבְדּוֹ בְּלִי פְּרִיקַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם רֶגַע אֶחָד; וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה "כָּל הַמְקַבֵּל עָלָיו עוֹל תּוֹרָה – פּוֹרְקִין מִמֶּנּוּ עוֹל מַלְכוּת וְכוּלֵי" אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ג, ה, זָכָה לְמַלְכוּת שֶׁהוּא הַחֵירוּת הַגָּמוּר, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מָגֵן לוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: “You shall be a blessing”—with you they conclude, as the Sages said; and likewise with King David. Abraham is the beginning of creation. “Only three are called fathers”: they are the fathers of the world and the beginning of the recognition of divinity. Abraham is the father of them all, “the father of a multitude of nations.” The title father is included in his name, for father means expansion into branches, the quality of kindness that expands. The Zohar says, “Abba founded the daughter.” As explained elsewhere, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David correspond to father, mother, son, and daughter. “The final act was first in thought”: King David, who is the Messiah, is the culmination of creation. Therefore the blessing’s concluding seal with him relates to the beginning of thought. The seal is “Shield.” So too with the festivals: recognition begins at Pesach, the month of spring, when the reception of divinity begins; it concludes at the Festival of Ingathering, Sukkot, a shelter and refuge expressing confidence that God protects the person. This comes after the completion of the summer’s service: King David’s level in the name of Lordship, “I have set God before me always,” like a master before his servant, without casting off the kingdom of Heaven for even a moment. Through this, “Whoever accepts the yoke of Torah has the yoke of government removed from him,” and so forth. He merits kingship, which is complete freedom, and the blessed God shields him.
records.explanation: Kometz HaMinchah explains the two seals through “the final act was first in thought.” Abraham begins the disclosure of divinity, while David’s kingship is its culmination; the final shield therefore belongs already to the beginning. The progression from Pesach to Sukkot supplies a further example of recognition reaching settled protection. This develops the structure of Rav Tzadok’s closing argument without replacing its particular account of protection from sin.

records.themeTitle: Prayer for the Divine Name and the fullness of repair
records.themeSummary: David asks for restoration so that God’s Name will not be profaned. Rav Tzadok elsewhere distinguishes removing sins for the sake of that Name from the fuller transformation achieved through repentance from love.
records.originHebrew: "נַפְשִׁי יְשׁוֹבֵב יַנְחֵנִי בְמַעְגְּלֵי צֶדֶק לְמַעַן שְׁמוֹ", הוּא עַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וָאַעַשׂ לְמַעַן שְׁמִי לְבִלְתִּי הֵחֵל לְעֵינֵי הַגּוֹיִם", כִּי כְּשֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל אֵינָם כָּרָאוּי נִתְחַלֵּל שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בֵּין הָאוּמּוֹת, כִּדְכְתִיב: "בֶּאֱמֹר לָהֶם עַם ה' אֵלֶּה וּמֵאַרְצוֹ יָצָאוּ", וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: "לָכֵן אֱמֹר לְבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל: לֹא לְמַעַנְכֶם אֲנִי עֹשֶׂה בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי אִם לְשֵׁם קָדְשִׁי וְגוֹמֵר", וְכֵן הִתְפַּלֵּל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "לֹא לָנוּ כִּי לְשִׁמְךָ תֵּן כָּבוֹד וְגוֹמֵר", הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִתְחַלֵּל שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּדְכְתִיב: "לָמָּה יֹאמְרוּ הַגּוֹיִם אַיֵּה נָא אֱלֹהֵיהֶם".
records.originEnglish: “He restores my soul; He guides me in paths of righteousness for the sake of His Name.” This follows the pattern of what is said: “I acted for the sake of My Name, so that it should not be profaned before the nations.” For when Israel does not act as it should, His blessed Name is profaned among the nations, as it is written: “When they said of them, ‘These are the Lord’s people, yet they have left His land.’” Of this it is said: “Therefore say to the house of Israel: It is not for your sake that I act, house of Israel, but for My holy Name,” and so forth. King David, of blessed memory, similarly prayed: “Not for us … but to Your Name give honor,” and so forth—that His blessed Name should not be profaned, as it is written: “Why should the nations say, ‘Where, then, is their God?’”
records.targetHebrew: אֲבָל שְׁלֵמוּת הַתִּקּוּן כְּשֶׁיִּזְכֶּה לִתְשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵימָה, שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, עַד דַּעֲלֵיהֶם הוּא חַיֹּה יִחְיֶה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפֶרֶק יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים (יוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳); וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי שֶׁלְּבָבוֹ בּוֹעֵר כְּאֵשׁ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַד שֶׁנִּשְׂרָף וְנִכְלָה כָּל הַפְּסֹלֶת וְהָרָע שֶׁבַּלֵּב וְנַעֲשָׂה כֻּלּוֹ קֹדֶשׁ לַה', מִמֵּילָא מִתְגַּלֶּה דְּגַם: "כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָּנוּ", וְכָל הַחֲטָאִים הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ "עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ" דִּגְדוֹלָה מִמִּצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ (נָזִיר כ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳), וְהַחֲטָאִים כַּשָּׁנִים נַעֲשָׂה מֵהֶם לְבוּשׁ שָׁנִים דְּמִצְוֹת, וּבָזֶה הוּא נִצּוּחַ וְאָבְדַן שֹׁרֶשׁ כָּל הָרַע וְכֹחַ הָאֻמּוֹת וֶאֱדוֹם; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "מִי זֶה בָּא מֵאֱדוֹם חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁכִּבְיָכוֹל לוֹבֵשׁ לְבוּשָׁן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל הַנַּעֲשֶׂה מֵחֲטָאֵיהֶם אַחַר שֶׁנִּזְדַּכְּכוּ וּמַזְהִירִים כַּשָּׁנִים. וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי יִצְחָק שֶׁאוֹמֵר: "פַּלְגָא עָלַי וּפַלְגָא עָלָךְ", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּפֶרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא (שַׁבָּת פ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳), וְלֹא כְּאַבְרָהָם וְיַעֲקֹב שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: "יִמָּחוּ עַל קְדֻשַּׁת שְׁמֶךָ"; וּפֵרְשׁוּ קַדְמוֹנֵינוּ דַּעֲוֹנוֹת קָאֵי, שֶׁיִּמָּחוּ בִּשְׁבִיל קְדֻשַּׁת הַשֵּׁם, שֶׁאִם אֵין לָנוּ זְכוּת יַעֲשֶׂה לְמַעַן שְׁמוֹ הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁנִּקְרָא עָלֵינוּ, וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "לֹא לָנוּ וְגוֹמֵר כִּי לְשִׁמְךָ תֵּן כָּבוֹד וְגוֹמֵר לָמָּה יֹאמְרוּ הַגּוֹיִם וְגוֹמֵר"; וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ שָׁם: לָא בְּסָבָא וְכוּלֵי, דְּעַדַיִן אֵין זֶה עֵצָה הָרְאוּיָה לִזְכוּתָן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּהֲגַם שֶׁיִּמָּחוּ הָעֲוֹנוֹת וְיִהְיוּ כְּאִלּוּ אֵינָם, אַכַּתִּי מָה הוֹעִילוּ בְּמַה שֶּׁנִּבְרְאוּ וְנִשְׁלְחוּ לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה;
records.targetEnglish: But repair is complete when one merits complete repentance, so that deliberate sins become merits, to the point that through them he shall truly live, as stated in the chapter Yom HaKippurim (Yoma 86b). This comes through his heart burning like fire for the blessed God until all the dross and evil in the heart are consumed and it becomes wholly holy to God. It consequently becomes apparent that “all our deeds You have performed for us,” and that all the sins follow the pattern of “a transgression for the sake of Heaven,” which is greater than a mitzvah performed without that intention (Nazir 23b). From sins like scarlet there is made a scarlet garment of mitzvot. This is the defeat and destruction of the root of all evil and the power of the nations and Edom, as it is written: “Who is this coming from Edom, with crimson garments,” and so forth: He, as it were, wears Israel’s garment, made from their sins after they have been purified and shine like scarlet. This comes through Isaac, who says, “Half upon me and half upon You,” as stated in the chapter Rabbi Akiva (Shabbat 89b), unlike Abraham and Jacob, who said there, “Let them be erased for the sanctity of Your Name.” Our predecessors explained that this refers to the sins: let them be erased for the sanctity of the Name, so that if we have no merit, He will act for His great Name that is called upon us. This follows the verse, “Not for us … but to Your Name give honor … why should the nations say,” and so forth. Of this they said there, “Neither in the old man …”: this is still not counsel adequate to Israel’s merit. Although the sins will be erased as if they did not exist, what have they gained by being created and sent into this world?
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim cites the same “not for us” prayer and explains the request that sins be erased for the sanctity of God’s Name even without personal merit. It then distinguishes that erasure from repentance whose burning love transforms the past into merit. This gives a precise place to the opening prayer in Lech Lecha and prepares its following account of a past whose meaning is ultimately disclosed; the two stages are not treated as interchangeable.
records.translationProvenance: New English translations of the unchanged canonical Hebrew excerpts, prepared for this editorial connection. The complete originating section and the complete target paragraph were read in context. This comparison does not claim that one author explicitly cites the other.

records.themeTitle: The ordered past and the continuing responsibility to choose
records.themeSummary: Future recognition of Divine guidance reaches even the troubled past. Its relation to moral choice becomes clearer when Rav Tzadok distinguishes the standpoint of Divine knowledge from the standpoint in which a person must act.
records.originHebrew: וְזֶה הוּא הַתְּפִלָּה גַּם כֵּן: "יַנְחֵנִי בְמַעְגְּלֵי צֶדֶק לְמַעַן שְׁמוֹ" – שֶׁלֹּא יִתְחַלֵּל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, יוֹלִיכֵנוּ בַּדֶּרֶךְ הָרָאוּי, כִּי כֹּל יָכוֹל ה', כָּל אֲשֶׁר חָפֵץ עָשָׂה. וְאַף עַכְשָׁיו אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ, וְאֵין כֹּחַ בְּשׁוּם נִבְרָא לַעֲשׂוֹת דָּבָר בְּלֹא רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "הָאֱלֹהִים הָרֹעֶה אֹתִי מֵעוֹדִי", וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר: "ה' רֹעִי וְגוֹמֵר". רַק שֶׁעַכְשָׁיו אֵינוֹ בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת, וּלְעָתִיד יִהְיֶה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁכָּל הֶעָבָר נַעֲשָׂה רַק מֵרְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ. וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "'אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים' – כַּשָּׁנִים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ" (שַׁבָּת פט עַמּוּד ב), כִּי הַכֹּל הָיָה מֵרְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ. וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "גַּם כִּי אֵלֵךְ וְגוֹמֵר לֹא אִירָא רָע כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי", כִּי מִצַּד עַצְמֵנוּ אֵין כֹּחַ לַעֲשׂוֹת מְאוּמָה.
records.originEnglish: This is also the prayer, “He guides me in paths of righteousness for the sake of His Name”: so that it should not be profaned, God forbid, let Him lead us in the proper way. For God can do all things; He does whatever He wills. Even now there is none besides Him, and no creature has power to do anything without His blessed will, as Jacob our father, of blessed memory, said, “The God who has shepherded me from my beginning,” and King David, of blessed memory, said, “The Lord is my shepherd,” and so forth. It is simply not revealed now. In the future it will be revealed that everything in the past occurred only through His blessed will. Of this they said: “‘If your sins are like years’—like these years that have been ordered and have come since the six days of Creation—‘they shall become white as snow’” (Shabbat 89b), for everything was through His blessed will. This is “Even when I walk … I shall fear no evil, for You are with me”: on our own we have no power to do anything.
records.targetHebrew: מ] עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַד שֶׁיָּאִיר ה' עֵינָיו שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁיַּכִּיר וְיָבִין שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁחָטָא הָיָה גַּם כֵּן בִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמַאֲמַר רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּרָכוֹת לא סוֹף עַמּוּד ב): ג' פְּסוּקִים וְכוּלֵי, "וְאַתָּה הֲסִבֹּתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית", "וַאֲשֶׁר הֲרֵעֹתִי" וְכוּלֵי. וּכְטַעַם יְדִיעָה וּבְחִירָה שֶׁבֵּיאַר הָאֲרִ"י זַ"ל בְּסוֹף סֵפֶר אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שֶׁקֶל כֶּסֶף, שֶׁשְּׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, כָּל אֶחָד בְּמָקוֹם בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ: בִּמְקוֹם הַבְּחִירָה שָׁם אֵין מָקוֹם לִידִיעָה, וּבִמְקוֹם הַיְדִיעָה שָׁם בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין מָקוֹם לַבְּחִירָה. וּכְשֶׁמַּשִּׂיג לְאוֹר זֶה הָעָצוּם, אָז שָׁבוּ כָּל זְדוֹנוֹתָיו בִּלְתִּי יוֹצְאִים מֵעוֹמֶק יְדִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְהוּא וְדַעְתּוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ הַכֹּל אֶחָד. וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רָצָה כֵּן, הֲרֵי הַכֹּל זְכִיּוֹת, וְזוֹכֶה לְכַפָּרָה גְּמוּרָה שֶׁבְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, שֶׁזֶּה סוֹד הַשָּׂעִיר לַעֲזָאזֵל, שֶׁאִלּוּ עֲשָׂאוּהוּ הָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ הָיָה עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה גָּמוּר, וְהוּא "לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ" שֶׁהוּא יְסוֹד כָּל הַמִּצְווֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה וְכָל הָעֲבֵירוֹת וְהַהֲסָרוֹת מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ. רַק שֶׁהַשָּׂעִיר הוּא עַל יְדֵי רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא מִצְוָה לְשַׁלְּחוֹ לוֹ, נַעֲשָׂה עוֹד מִצְוָה וְלֹא עֲבֵירָה. וְכָךְ פֵּירְשׁוּהוּ רַבּוֹתֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (פִּרְקֵי דְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר פֶּרֶק מו), וְעַיֵּין בָּרַמְבַּ"ן פָּרָשַׁת אַחֲרֵי, שֶׁאָנוּ נוֹתְנִים חֵלֶק לַעֲזָאזֵל שֶׁהוּא הָרַע מִצַּד מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צִוָּה לָתֵת לוֹ, וְנִמְצָא הָעֲבֵירָה מִצְוָה:
records.targetEnglish: The essence of repentance is that God should illuminate a person’s eyes until deliberate sins become merits. This means that he recognizes and understands that everything in which he sinned was also within the blessed God’s will, as our Sages taught concerning three verses, including “You have turned their hearts backward” and “whom I have harmed” (Berakhot 31b). This accords with knowledge and choice, as the Ari explained at the end of Sefer Arba Meot Shekel Kesef: both are true, each in its own domain. In the domain of choice there is no place for knowledge; in the domain of knowledge there is indeed no place for choice. When one attains this immense light, all his deliberate sins are seen as not departing from the depth of God’s knowledge; He, His knowledge, and His will are all one. Since the blessed God willed it thus, everything is merit, and he attains the complete atonement of Yom Kippur. This is the mystery of the goat sent to Azazel: had a person performed this on his own initiative, he would have been an outright idolater, violating “You shall have no other gods,” the foundation of all prohibitions, transgressions, and departures from the blessed God’s will. But because the goat is sent through the blessed God’s will—He commands that it be sent there—it becomes a mitzvah rather than a transgression. Thus our Sages explained it in Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, chapter 46; see Ramban on Acharei Mot. We give a portion to Azazel, which is evil, because the blessed God commanded that it be given; thus what would be a transgression becomes a mitzvah.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik explains the same retrospective recognition through two true standpoints: knowledge and choice. Its example of the commanded Azazel rite makes the boundary concrete—a Divine command cannot be replaced by personal initiative. Read alongside Lech Lecha’s closing demand for strenuous effort, this explains why recognition that the past lay within Divine will does not authorize following one’s desires in the present.

records.themeTitle: The Shepherd’s constant guidance and our recognition of it
records.themeSummary: Jacob’s and David’s words name a guidance that never ceases. Mei HaShiloach explains the corresponding work of asking to recognize God’s will afresh in each particular action.
records.originHebrew: וְאַף עַכְשָׁיו אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ, וְאֵין כֹּחַ בְּשׁוּם נִבְרָא לַעֲשׂוֹת דָּבָר בְּלֹא רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "הָאֱלֹהִים הָרֹעֶה אֹתִי מֵעוֹדִי", וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר: "ה' רֹעִי וְגוֹמֵר". רַק שֶׁעַכְשָׁיו אֵינוֹ בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת, וּלְעָתִיד יִהְיֶה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁכָּל הֶעָבָר נַעֲשָׂה רַק מֵרְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.originEnglish: Even now there is none besides Him, and no creature has power to do anything without His blessed will, as Jacob our father, of blessed memory, said, “The God who has shepherded me from my beginning,” and King David, of blessed memory, said, “The Lord is my shepherd,” and so forth. It is simply not revealed now. In the future it will be revealed that everything in the past occurred only through His blessed will.
records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayechi 3
records.targetHebrew: וַיֹּאמֶר הָאֱלֹקִים אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלְּכוּ אֲבוֹתַי לְפָנָיו הָאֱלֹקִים הָרוֹעֶה אוֹתִי מֵעוֹדִי. הַיְינוּ שֶׁיַּעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ הָיָה מַקְטִין עַצְמוֹ נֶגֶד אֲבוֹתָיו אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק, וְאָמַר כִּי לָהֶם הָיָה חָכְמָה וּבִינָה גְּדוֹלָה מְאֹד עַד כִּי הִרְחִיבוּ אֶת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵעַצְמָם, וְאַף אִם פָּתַח לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ פֶּתַח קָטָן, הָיוּ מַרְחִיבִים וּמִתְפַּשְּׁטִים אוֹתוֹ בְּחָכְמָתָם כְּדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹן בּוֹרְאָם, וְהֵבִינוּ אַף בְּדָבָר שֶׁלֹּא הֵאִיר לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְפֹרָשׁ, וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלְּכוּ" הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיוּ הוֹלְכִים בְּכֹחָם. אֲבָל אֲנִי, "הָאֱלֹקִים הָרוֹעֶה אוֹתִי מֵעוֹדִי עַד הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה", הַיְינוּ בְּכָל פְּרָט מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁאֲנִי עוֹשֶׂה, אֲנִי צָרִיךְ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יָאִיר עֵינַי אֵיךְ הוּא רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְאַף בְּזֶה הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁרָאִיתִי אֵיךְ הוּא רְצוֹנוֹ, אִם רְצוֹנוֹ לְשַׁנּוֹתָהּ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ אֲנִי לִרְאוֹת גַּם בַּפַּעַם הַשֵּׁנִית אֵיךְ הוּא רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבֶאֱמֶת בְּזֶה הָעִנְיָן הָיָה יַעֲקֹב הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבָּאָבוֹת כִּי זֹאת הִיא מַדְרֵגָה גְּדוֹלָה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַנְהִיג אֶת הָאָדָם תָּמִיד, וְזֹאת הָיְתָה תְּפִלַּת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם (תְּהִלִּים כָּף גִּימֶל, אָלֶף) "הַשֵּׁם רוֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר", הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא אַחְסִיר הַשְׁגָּחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עָלַי וְרַק שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רוֹעֶה אוֹתִי תָּמִיד וְגַם אֲנִי אַכִּיר תָּמִיד שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא רוֹעִי, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּטוּבוֹ מַנְהִיג כָּל דָּבָר, אַךְ שֶׁהָאָדָם מַחְזִיר פָּנָיו וְאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לְצַפּוֹת וּלְהִתְפַּלֵּל, וּבְעֵת שֶׁהָאָדָם יִתְפַּלֵּל תְּפִלָּה שְׁלֵימָה אָז תֵּיכֶף יֵעָנֶה, וְיִרְאֶה כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הָרוֹעֶה וְזֶה פֵּירוּשׁ "לֹא אֶחְסָר" הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא אַחְזִיר פָּנַי מִמֶּנּוּ.
records.targetEnglish: “He said: The God before whom my fathers walked, the God who has shepherded me from my beginning.” Jacob our father was making himself small before his fathers Abraham and Isaac. He said that they possessed very great wisdom and understanding, so that they expanded the expression of the blessed God’s will on their own: even if God opened a small opening for them, they broadened it through their wisdom in order to do their Creator’s will, understanding even something God had not explicitly illuminated for them. This is “before whom they walked”: they walked with their own power. “But I—the God who has shepherded me from my beginning until this day”: in every particular act that I perform, I need the blessed God to open my eyes to what His will is. Even in an act in which I have already seen His will, if I am to repeat it, I must nevertheless see again, on the second occasion, what His blessed will is. In truth, in this respect Jacob was the greatest of the Patriarchs, for it is a great level that the blessed God should constantly guide a person. This was King David’s prayer, “The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not lack” (Psalms 23:1): may I never lack God’s providence over me, but may He constantly shepherd me, and may I also constantly recognize that He is my shepherd. For in His goodness the blessed God guides everything, but a person turns his face away and does not wish to look toward Him and pray. When a person prays a complete prayer, he is answered immediately and sees that the blessed God is the shepherd. This is “I shall not lack”: that I should not turn my face away from Him.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach interprets the same two shepherd verses together. He distinguishes God’s constant guidance from the person’s turning toward it through attention and prayer, and even requires fresh discernment when an apparently familiar action recurs. This illuminates Lech Lecha’s distinction between guidance that already exists and guidance that has become apparent, while preserving the section’s active response of seeking and praying.

records.themeTitle: After the work of return, recognizing its Divine source
records.themeSummary: The admission that we have no independent power follows a call for righteous guidance. Sod Yesharim places this admission after the concrete labor of repentance, making its sequence explicit.
records.originHebrew: וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ: "'אִם יִהְיוּ חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים' – כַּשָּׁנִים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ" (שַׁבָּת פט עַמּוּד ב), כִּי הַכֹּל הָיָה מֵרְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ. וְזֶה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "גַּם כִּי אֵלֵךְ וְגוֹמֵר לֹא אִירָא רָע כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי", כִּי מִצַּד עַצְמֵנוּ אֵין כֹּחַ לַעֲשׂוֹת מְאוּמָה.
records.originEnglish: Of this they said: “‘If your sins are like years’—like these years that have been ordered and have come since the six days of Creation—‘they shall become white as snow’” (Shabbat 89b), for everything was through His blessed will. This is “Even when I walk … I shall fear no evil, for You are with me”: on our own we have no power to do anything.
records.targetHebrew: וזה הענין הוא נמי ביום כפור כי אחר כל העבודות החזקות מימי התשובה הקודמים שהם כדאיתא בירושלמי (יומא) נגד הפסוק רחצו הזכו וכו' היינו שבאלו העשרה ימים מבררים ישראל עצמם ורוחצים ומנקים את לבבם מכל רע עד מקום שכח ידם מגיע ואח"כ כשמגיע יום כפור אומרים ישראל שאפילו זה הכח לברר ולנקות את הלב אינו ג"כ בכח ידם ואין לנו שום דבר שנהיה יכולים לבטוח ולסמוך עליו ואין לנו להשען על שום עבודה ואצל מי נלך עכשיו רק על אבינו מלכנו שבשמים וזה הוא שאנו אומרים אחר כל התפלות של זה היום אבינו מלכנו וגו' אמר הקב"ה הואיל ותליתם עצמכם בי אם יהיו חטאיכם כשנים כשלג ילבינו.
records.targetEnglish: This is also the matter on Yom Kippur. After all the strenuous services of the preceding days of repentance—which the Jerusalem Talmud in Yoma sets against the verse “Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean,” and so forth—Israel refines itself during these ten days, washing and cleaning the heart of all evil as far as its power can reach. Then, when Yom Kippur arrives, Israel says that even this power to refine and cleanse the heart is not within its own power. We have nothing upon which we can rely and place our trust; we cannot lean upon any service. To whom can we turn now? Only to our Father and King in Heaven. This is why, after all the prayers of this day, we say, “Our Father, our King,” and so forth. The Holy One, blessed be He, says: “Since you have made yourselves dependent upon Me, though your sins be like scarlet, they shall become white as snow.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim applies the same promise that scarlet sins become white to Yom Kippur: Israel first washes and refines the heart as far as human capacity reaches, and then recognizes that even this capacity came from God. That order helps read Lech Lecha’s statement of dependence together with its final warning against abandoning effort. The target explains dependence after labor without replacing Rav Tzadok’s additional interpretation of the ordered years of Creation.

records.themeTitle: Why trust can remain after a fall
records.themeSummary: The enduring life associated with Jacob grounds Israel’s confidence even after failure. Resisei Layla spells out the difference between grave deterioration in conduct and a root whose bond has not been severed.
records.originHebrew: וְאַחַר כָּךְ: "כִּי לְשִׁמְךָ תֵּן כָּבוֹד עַל חַסְדְּךָ עַל אֲמִתֶּךָ" – הַיְינוּ מִדַּת אַבְרָהָם וְיַעֲקֹב: "חַסְדְּךָ" מְרַמֵּז לְמִדַּת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ שֶׁהָיָה מִדַּת חֶסֶד, הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה; וּמִדַּת יַעֲקֹב – "אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב", חַיּוּת שֶׁאֵין לָהּ הֶפְסֵק, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ. וְסִיֵּים הַכָּתוּב: "יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּטַח בַּה', עֶזְרָם וּמָגִנָּם הוּא וְגוֹמֵר", כִּי כְּפִי מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם בּוֹטְחִים שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ עָבַר מַה שֶּׁעָבַר, וְ"גַם כִּי אֵלֵךְ וְגוֹמֵר" – הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹזֵר לְהוֹצִיאָם וּלְהַצִּילָם, וּמָגֵן שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל שׁוּם דָּבָר רַע לִפְגּוֹעַ בָּהֶם.
records.originEnglish: Afterward: “But to Your Name give honor, for Your kindness and Your truth”—these are the qualities of Abraham and Jacob. “Your kindness” alludes to Abraham our father, whose quality was kindness, the expansion of holiness; Jacob’s quality is “truth to Jacob,” life that has no interruption, as we explained. The verse concludes: “Israel, trust in the Lord; He is their help and their shield,” and so forth. In keeping with Israel’s stature, they trust that even if whatever has passed has passed, and “even when I walk,” and so forth, the blessed God helps to bring them out and rescue them, and shields them so that no evil thing can strike them.
records.targetHebrew: וְזֶהוּ הַשִּׂמְחָה תְּמִידִית שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָאִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי מַה שֶּׁנּוֹצַר יְהוּדִי, וְנִיטַּע תּוֹךְ מַטַּע ה' לְהִתְפָּאֵר זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב, דְּזוֹ שִׂמְחָה שֶׁאֵין עֶצֶב עִמָּהּ, וְאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר הַחוֹצֵץ וּמְעַכֵּב בְּעַד שִׂמְחָה זוֹ מַה שֶּׁזָּכָה לִהְיוֹת לוֹ חֵלֶק בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים. וַאֲפִילּוּ נִשְׁתַּקַּע בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּקַּע וְהִגְדִּיל עֲווֹנוֹת לְאֵין שִׁיעוּר, עֲדַיִן לֹא נִיתַּק וְנִכְרַת דְּבֵיקוּת שָׁרְשׁוֹ בִּמְקוֹרָהּ, שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּזֶרַע יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהָיְתָה מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה וְ"לֹא יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח". וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּשֵׁם כְּלַל הַכְּנֵסִיָּה בִּהְיוֹתָם בְּתַכְלִית הַיְרִידָה וְהַשִּׁפְלוּת: "גַּם כִּי אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת לֹא אִירָא רָע כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי" (תְּהִלִּים כג, ד). שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ הוֹלֵךְ בַּדְּיוֹטָא הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה שֶׁבַּמְּבוֹאוֹת הָאֲפֵלוֹת דְּהִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת חֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה וַהֲבָלָיו, שֶׁהֵם דִּמְיוֹנוֹת שֶׁל תֹּהוּ וְעַד אַרְגִּיעָה וּמְכוּנִים בְּ"גֵיא צַלְמָוֶת", לֹא אִירַע רַע כְּלָל מֵאַחַר דְּ"אַתָּה עִמָּדִי", אֲפִילּוּ אַפּוּם מַחְתַּרְתָּא, אִם כֵּן "הוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אוֹרְחוֹתָיו".
records.targetEnglish: This is the constant joy of a person of Israel in having been created a Jew and planted among God’s planting for glory, the seed of Jacob. It is a joy with no sadness alongside it: nothing interposes or prevents this joy at having merited a portion in the living God. Even if one has sunk wherever he has sunk and multiplied sins beyond measure, the attachment of his root to its source has still not been severed or cut off. That is impossible among the descendants of Jacob our father, whose bed was complete, and “none of the banished will remain banished from Him.” This follows King David’s words on behalf of the entire congregation at its deepest descent and lowliness: “Even when I walk in the valley of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, for You are with me” (Psalms 23:4). Even if one walks in the lowest level of the dark alleys of absorption in this world’s desires and vanities—empty imaginings that last only a moment and are called the “valley of the shadow of death”—no evil has occurred at all, since “You are with me,” even at the mouth of a burglar’s tunnel. If so, “He will make his paths straight.”
records.explanation: Resisei Layla directly explains why “whatever has passed” need not destroy trust: even severe sin has not cut off the root of Jacob’s descendants from its source. It reads the same valley-of-death verse on that basis. The surrounding paragraph keeps this joy inside Divine service joined to awe, while Lech Lecha’s closing paragraph requires effort and prayer; the enduring bond supports return rather than making conduct immaterial.

records.themeTitle: The capacity to hope survives subsequent exile
records.themeSummary: Israel trusts in help despite what has happened. Tiferet Yosef explains how the first redemption leaves a lasting power to hope and work toward later redemption.
records.originHebrew: וְסִיֵּים הַכָּתוּב: "יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּטַח בַּה', עֶזְרָם וּמָגִנָּם הוּא וְגוֹמֵר", כִּי כְּפִי מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם בּוֹטְחִים שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ עָבַר מַה שֶּׁעָבַר, וְ"גַם כִּי אֵלֵךְ וְגוֹמֵר" – הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עוֹזֵר לְהוֹצִיאָם וּלְהַצִּילָם, וּמָגֵן שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל שׁוּם דָּבָר רַע לִפְגּוֹעַ בָּהֶם.
records.originEnglish: The verse concludes: “Israel, trust in the Lord; He is their help and their shield,” and so forth. In keeping with Israel’s stature, they trust that even if whatever has passed has passed, and “even when I walk,” and so forth, the blessed God helps to bring them out and rescue them, and shields them so that no evil thing can strike them.
records.targetHebrew: והענין בזה שע"י הקיווי והציפוי, שישראל מקווים ומיחלים תמיד על הגאולה שתהיה במהרה בימינו, נחשב להם כאילו הם הושיעו לעצמם, ובאמת הכח של הקיווי בא להם ע"י גאולת מצרים, היינו שבגלות מצרים גבר עליהם ההסתר עד מאד, עד היכן שלא היה בשום אחד מישראל שום ציפוי וחשק לגאולה, ומעת שהשי"ת גאל אותנו נטע בלבינו זה הכח, שמעתה יהיה כל אחד מישראל מקוה ומצפה לגאולת עולם. וזה שאומרים גאל ישראל היינו גאולת מצרים, וזה שאומרים גואל ישראל היינו גאולה העתידה להיות, שהשי"ת עוסק תמיד בגאולה זאת, היינו ע"י כח הקיווי שנטע בלבינו שנהיה מקוים ומיחלים לגאולה העתידה. וכמו שאנו אומרים ויוצא את עמו ישראל מתוכם לחרות עולם, והרי כמה גליות עברו עלינו אחר גאולת מצרים ועדיין לא נושענו. אכן לפי מה שנתבאר שע"י גאולת מצרים קבע השי"ת בלב ישראל כח הקיווי והציפוי ולהיות מיחלים תמיד לגאולה העתידה, וזה שאומרים גואל ישראל שהשי"ת עוסק תמיד בגאולה זאת, היינו ע"י הקיווי שבלב ישראל שמיחלים תמיד לגאולה, בזכות זה יהיו נגאלים ויהיה נקרא הגאולה על שמם. וכל זה היה לנו ע"י גאולת מצרים.
records.targetEnglish: The meaning is that through the hope and expectation with which Israel constantly hopes and waits for redemption—may it come speedily in our days—it is counted to them as though they had saved themselves. In truth, the power to hope came to them through the redemption from Egypt. In the Egyptian exile concealment had become so overwhelming that no one in Israel had any expectation or desire for redemption. From the time the blessed God redeemed us, He planted this power in our hearts: henceforth each person of Israel would hope and wait for everlasting redemption. Thus “Who redeemed Israel” refers to the redemption from Egypt; “Who redeems Israel” refers to the future redemption, with which the blessed God is constantly occupied, through the power of hope He planted in our hearts so that we would hope and await it. We say, “He brought His people Israel out from among them to everlasting freedom”; yet how many exiles have passed over us since the redemption from Egypt, and we have still not been saved! But as explained, through the redemption from Egypt God fixed in Israel’s heart the power to hope, expect, and continually await the future redemption. This is “Who redeems Israel”: God is constantly occupied with that redemption through the hope in Israel’s heart. In this merit they will be redeemed, and the redemption will be called by their name. All this came to us through the redemption from Egypt.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef asks how the Exodus could be called everlasting freedom when further exiles followed. His answer identifies an enduring gift within an unfinished history: the capacity to hope for redemption, through which Israel’s service is counted as its own. This adds a concrete account of the trust that Lech Lecha associates with unbroken life, without claiming that later distress has already ceased.

records.themeTitle: How Torah gives strength against the inclination
records.themeSummary: Rav Tzadok names Divine help and Torah’s shield as two means of rescue. Tzidkat HaTzadik explains their meeting point: God helps through the Torah light that He makes available to the person.
records.originHebrew: וְהֵם שְׁנֵי עִנְיָנִים שֶׁבָּהֶם אָדָם נִיצּוֹל מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע: "עֵזֶר" – עַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (סֻכָּה נב עַמּוּד ב): "יִצְרוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם מִתְגַּבֵּר עָלָיו בְּכָל יוֹם וְכוּלֵי, וְאִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁעוֹזְרוֹ אֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לוֹ"; וּ"מָגֵן" הוּא מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ: "אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנוּוָול זֶה – מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ", וְדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה נִקְרְאוּ "מָגֵן".
records.originEnglish: These are two matters through which a person is rescued from the evil inclination. “Help” follows what they said (Sukkah 52b): “A person’s inclination grows stronger against him every day … and were the Holy One, blessed be He, not to help him, he could not overcome it.” The “shield” is what they said: “If this vile one encounters you, draw it into the study hall”; words of Torah are called a shield.
records.targetHebrew: [קפז] הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה הֵם עֹז לָאָדָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וְהַחָכְמָה תָּעֹז [לֶחָכָם]" (קֹהֶלֶת ז, יט), וְ"אֵיזֶהוּ גִבּוֹר? הַכּוֹבֵשׁ [אֶת יִצְרוֹ]" (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד, א), שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (קִדּוּשִׁין ל:): מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע, בָּרָאתִי תוֹרָה וְכוּלֵי; שֶׁזֶּהוּ "אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ וְכוּלֵי" (סֻכָּה נב:), וְהָעֵזֶר וְהַסַּיַּעְתָּא הוּא עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁמֵּאִיר לוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: Words of Torah give a person strength, as it is written: “Wisdom gives strength [to the wise]” (Ecclesiastes 7:19), and “Who is mighty? One who subdues [his inclination]” (Avot 4:1). Through Torah he overcomes his inclination, as it is stated (Kiddushin 30b), “Draw it into the study hall,” and “I created the evil inclination; I created Torah,” and so forth. This is “Were the Holy One, blessed be He, not to help him,” and so forth (Sukkah 52b): the help and assistance come through the words of Torah that He illuminates for him.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik joins the two teachings that Lech Lecha distinguishes: being drawn into Torah study and receiving God’s indispensable help. It identifies the help as Torah made luminous to the person, rather than the bare fact of entering a study hall. This also prepares the next paragraph of Lech Lecha, where a hardened heart can still need help to receive that light.

records.themeTitle: The obstacles that can remain inside Torah study
records.themeSummary: Jabez still prays for protection from the inclination while studying Torah. Rav Tzadok’s Vaetchanan discussion identifies discouragement and self-exaltation as two different ways its light can be obstructed.
records.originHebrew: אַךְ אַף כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ יוּכַל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע לְהִתְגַּבֵּר, וּמַקְשֶׁה לִבּוֹ לְבַל יִכָּנְסוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וּמַחְשִׁיךְ לְפָנָיו אוֹר, חַיּוּת וּקְדֻשַּׁת הַתּוֹרָה, וּמְבַלְבֵּל אֶת דַּעְתּוֹ. כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּיַעְבֵּץ, אַף שֶׁהָיָה מְנוּגָּב מִכָּל חֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְהָיָה עוֹסֵק תָּמִיד בַּתּוֹרָה, הִתְפַּלֵּל: "'לְבִלְתִּי עָצְבִּי' – שֶׁלֹּא יַשְׂגִּיבַנִי יֵצֶר הָרָע מִלִּשְׁנוֹת", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תְּמוּרָה טז עַמּוּד א), שֶׁאַף שֶׁהָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ הָיָה גַּם כֵּן מִתְיָירֵא מֵהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁלֹּא יְבַלְבֵּל דַּעְתּוֹ, וּלְזֶה צָרִיךְ עֶזְרָה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.originEnglish: Yet even when a person is in the study hall, the evil inclination can grow strong. It hardens his heart so that words of Torah do not enter, darkens the light, vitality, and holiness of Torah before him, and confuses his mind. We find this with Jabez: although he was emptied of all this world’s desires and constantly engaged in Torah, he prayed, “‘That it should not grieve me’—that the evil inclination should not overpower me and prevent my study,” as stated in Temurah 16a. Even while sitting in the study hall he feared that the evil inclination would confuse his mind. For this he needs help from the blessed God.
records.targetHebrew: כל גיא ינשא דהנה עיקר היצה"ר הוא ראשית גוים עמלק יצרא בישא ונא' עליו אשר קרך שהוא מכניס קרירות ועצב בלב האדם להתרשל מד"ת מצד שאין מעשיו כהוגן ולכן אין תורתו ועבודתו פועלים כלום. וכמו שמצינו ביעבץ הגם שהוא ע"י פלפולו החזיר התורה שנשתכחה בימי אבלו של משה עכ"ז התפלל לבלתי עצבי שלא ישגבני יצה"ר מלשנות (כמ"ש תמורה ט"ז.) וע"ז נצרך חיזוק בלב כמו שנא' ויגבה לבו בדרכי ה' שיאמין שבתורתו מוסיף כח למעלה כמו"ש תנו עוז לאלהים ע"ז נאמר הבטחה כל גיא ינשא. וכל הר וגבעה ישפלו הוא השפלת היצה"ר שנמשל להר והוא מה שמכניס התנשאות בלב. והי' העקוב למישור היינו ליישר גם הלב כסיל לשמאלו כמו שנא' ולישרי לב שמחה. ונגלה כבוד ה' וראו כל בשר יחדיו כי פי ה' דבר שיתגלה בחוש שהקול הקורא בלב האדם הוא ממש פי ה' הנותן כח התעוררות בלבו.
records.targetEnglish: “Every valley shall be lifted.” The root of the evil inclination is “Amalek, first of the nations,” the evil inclination of which it is said, “who cooled you”: it brings coldness and sadness into a person’s heart, making him slacken in Torah study because his deeds are improper and therefore his Torah and service supposedly accomplish nothing. We find this with Jabez: although through his reasoning he restored the Torah forgotten during the mourning for Moses, he nevertheless prayed, “‘That it should not grieve me’—that the evil inclination should not overpower me and prevent my study” (Temurah 16a). For this, the heart needs strengthening, as it is said, “His heart was lifted in the ways of the Lord”: one must believe that through one’s Torah one adds strength above, as it is said, “Give strength to God.” For this comes the promise, “Every valley shall be lifted.” “Every mountain and hill shall be lowered” means lowering the evil inclination, likened to a mountain, that introduces self-exaltation into the heart. “The crooked shall become straight” means straightening also the fool’s heart on the left, as it is said, “And joy for the upright of heart.” “The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see together that the mouth of the Lord has spoken”: it will become tangibly revealed that the voice calling within a person’s heart is truly God’s mouth, giving the power of awakening in his heart.
records.explanation: The Vaetchanan passage interprets Jabez’s same prayer through a specific inward obstacle: the thought that defective conduct makes one’s Torah worthless, which chills further study. Its following clause also lowers the pride that the opposite response could produce. Together these details illuminate the hardened heart and obscured Torah light in Lech Lecha, while identifying the strengthening voice itself as God’s gift.

records.targetEnglish: Afterward: “May Your hand be with me” (I Chronicles 4:10)—that it should not be forgotten but remain in his possession. This is through “Your hand”: “your hand,” written with the extra letter heh, is interpreted as “the weak hand” (Menachot 37a), but “Your hand” here means the right hand. They said in Berakhot 6a, “At His right hand”—this is Torah, and so forth: God’s right hand imparts words of Torah. When it is with me, forgetting is impossible, for it continually imparts them. Because he asked for permanence, he immediately attached to this the request for companions, who maintain Torah in his possession, as explained above in paragraph 185. He placed the student before the companion because this was after the passing of Moses our teacher; see the Talmud there. Joshua had been appointed leader, occupied with allotting the land, and another occupation had begun. But Jabez—Othniel—had a heart trembling with desire for Torah; see there that he was sharper in reasoning than Joshua. He had neither companions nor students, so he first asked for blessing in Torah, since he was alone without teacher, companion, or student. Immediately with the blessing he had to ask for students, through whom he could become a vessel holding blessing. After the blessing he needed to ask for permanence and that he should not forget; then he asked for companions. Afterward, lest some sin interfere, he asked, “And keep me from evil, that it should not grieve me,” as our Sages explained there. Immediately, “God brought about what he asked.” Blessing, students, and companions could indeed come immediately in the plain sense. But permanence and protection from sin would apparently become known only at life’s end, when he saw that they had endured throughout his life. It seems that even this can be felt in the heart: when the words of Torah are fixed and enduring, he will not move from them, and transgression will not extinguish them, because there is enough in them to shatter the evil inclination. “Wisdom gives strength to the wise” (Ecclesiastes 7:19) and removes the fear that sin might interfere—the fear attributed to Jacob our father (Berakhot 4a). Someone whose strength comes from words of Torah is freed from every kind of fear.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik reads the order of Jabez’s petitions: blessing in Torah and students, then preservation with companions, then protection from sin. Its interpretation of God’s hand as continually imparting Torah explains why an accomplished scholar still asks for help. The ending describes the settled strength sought by that prayer; Lech Lecha emphasizes the danger that makes the request necessary.

records.themeTitle: When Torah still requires a further examination of the heart
records.themeSummary: Torah can confront desire while the learner remains vulnerable to confusion. Mei HaShiloach explains why the examination sometimes must continue through Shema and the remembrance of death.
records.originHebrew: אַךְ אַף כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ יוּכַל הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע לְהִתְגַּבֵּר, וּמַקְשֶׁה לִבּוֹ לְבַל יִכָּנְסוּ דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, וּמַחְשִׁיךְ לְפָנָיו אוֹר, חַיּוּת וּקְדֻשַּׁת הַתּוֹרָה, וּמְבַלְבֵּל אֶת דַּעְתּוֹ. כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּיַעְבֵּץ, אַף שֶׁהָיָה מְנוּגָּב מִכָּל חֶמְדּוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְהָיָה עוֹסֵק תָּמִיד בַּתּוֹרָה, הִתְפַּלֵּל: "'לְבִלְתִּי עָצְבִּי' – שֶׁלֹּא יַשְׂגִּיבַנִי יֵצֶר הָרָע מִלִּשְׁנוֹת", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (תְּמוּרָה טז עַמּוּד א), שֶׁאַף שֶׁהָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ הָיָה גַּם כֵּן מִתְיָירֵא מֵהַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁלֹּא יְבַלְבֵּל דַּעְתּוֹ, וּלְזֶה צָרִיךְ עֶזְרָה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ.
records.originEnglish: Yet even when a person is in the study hall, the evil inclination can grow strong. It hardens his heart so that words of Torah do not enter, darkens the light, vitality, and holiness of Torah before him, and confuses his mind. We find this with Jabez: although he was emptied of all this world’s desires and constantly engaged in Torah, he prayed, “‘That it should not grieve me’—that the evil inclination should not overpower me and prevent my study,” as stated in Temurah 16a. Even while sitting in the study hall he feared that the evil inclination would confuse his mind. For this he needs help from the blessed God.

וְשָׁם נֶאֱמַר לוֹ הַמַּאֲמָר "אָנֹכִי אַעַלְךָ גַם עָלֹה" אֲשֶׁר הוּא נֶגֶד הַמַּאֲמָר "אָנֹכִי הַשֵּׁם אֱלֹקֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִיךָ", רַק שָׁם הוּא לֶעָבָר וְהָכָא הוּא לֶעָתִיד, וְגַם מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר "וְאֶת יְהוּדָא שָׁלַח לְפָנָיו" וּפֵירְשׁוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (מִדְרָשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא וַיִּגַּשׁ יוֹד אָלֶף) לְתַקֵּן לוֹ בֵּית תַּלְמוּד הָיָה גַּם כֵּן מֵעִנְיָן הַלָּזֶה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ בֵּירֵר בַּבֵּירֵר הַשְּׁלִישִׁי וַיֵּבְךְּ עַל צַוָּארָיו עוֹד וְדָרְשׁוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מְלַמֵּד שֶׁקָּרָא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע, וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמַר לְיוֹסֵף "אָמוּתָה הַפָּעַם" הוּא נֶגֶד עֵצָה הָרְבִיעִית יַזְכִּיר לוֹ יוֹם הַמִּיתָה, וּכְשֶׁרָאָה יַעֲקֹב כִּי אַחַר כָּל אֵלֶּה נִשְׁאַר לוֹ הַשִּׂמְחָה, אָז הֵבִין כִּי מֵהַשֵּׁם הוּא וְהוּא שִׂמְחָה אֲמִיתִּית וְקַיָּים לָעַד.
records.targetEnglish: “If he has overcome it [through Torah], well; if not, let him recite the Shema.” For in words of Torah there can be self-exaltation: through Torah a person can embolden himself, and this can prevent him from reaching true discernment. The counsel is therefore to recite the Shema. The meaning of Shema follows the Talmud’s teaching (Taanit 31a) that in the future the Holy One, blessed be He, will make a circle for the righteous: all will see that everything is in God’s hand and that no one has any superiority or exaltation over another. A circle is round and has no end; this is what the Shema alludes to. “If he has overcome it, well; if not, let him remind himself of the day of death.” He should picture in his mind that now is the day of death. This differs from “let him agitate [the good inclination],” which was also interpreted along these lines: here he should imagine that the time of death is now, so that the desire and joy have no place. If, after all these tests, the desire or joy still remains in his heart, this is evidence that it comes from God and will endure forever. So it was with Jacob our father when he heard the news that Joseph was still alive and “Jacob’s spirit revived.” He feared that this joy might be only worldly joy, and therefore examined and refined himself through these tests. The first, “I shall go and see him before I die,” corresponds to “let a person always agitate,” as explained. The second, “He offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac,” corresponds to engaging in Torah. We bless each day, “Who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to engage in words of Torah”; in giving the Torah God is called Might—Moses heard from the mouth of Might (Megillah 31b), as is known to one who understands. There he was told, “I shall also surely bring you up,” corresponding to “I am the Lord your God who brought you out”; the latter speaks of the past, and the former of the future. “He sent Judah ahead of him,” which the Sages explain as preparing a house of study (Tanchuma, Vayigash 11), also belongs to this matter. He then examined himself through the third test, “He wept on his neck further,” which the Sages interpret as teaching that he recited the Shema. Afterward he said to Joseph, “Now I can die,” corresponding to the fourth counsel, to remember the day of death. When Jacob saw that the joy remained after all these tests, he understood that it came from God: it was true joy, enduring forever.
records.explanation: In his account of Jacob examining his joy at Joseph’s survival, Mei HaShiloach explains that Torah can itself become an occasion for self-exaltation, obstructing honest discernment. Shema removes that imagined superiority, and remembering death supplies a further test. This gives a concrete example of Lech Lecha’s claim that being in the study hall does not automatically remove the inclination; the comparison concerns testing the heart, with the target’s distinct account of Jacob’s joy retained.

records.themeTitle: The compassionate purpose of correction and its human limits
records.themeSummary: Worldly troubles are described as assistance toward service. Poked Akarim explains the paternal and medicinal analogy while still holding a person accountable for causing another person pain.
records.originHebrew: וְעֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא מַה שֶּׁמְּעוֹרְרָם לָשׁוּב עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג, קסח עַמּוּד א): "אָעָא דְּלָא סָלֵיק בֵּיהּ נְהוֹרָא עַד דִּיבַטְּשִׁין בֵּיהּ, וּכְדֵין נָהֵיר", "כִּי אֶת אֲשֶׁר יֶאֱהַב ה' יוֹכִיחַ, וּכְאָב אֶת בֵּן יִרְצֶה", וּכְתִיב: "כַּאֲשֶׁר יְיַסֵּר אִישׁ אֶת בְּנוֹ ה' אֱלֹהֶיךָ מְיַסְּרֶךָּ".
records.originEnglish: The blessed God’s help is what awakens them to return through afflictions, as stated in the holy Zohar (III, 168a): “Wood in which light does not rise must be struck, and then it shines.” “For the Lord reproves the one He loves, as a father the son in whom he delights”; and it is written, “As a man disciplines his son, the Lord your God disciplines you.”
records.targetHebrew: וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בְּחַנָּה, שֶׁהָיְתָה פְנִנָּה תַּחְתֶּיהָ, כְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה (בְּמִדְרַשׁ שְׁמוּאֵל פֶּרֶק ה׳, וּבְרַשִׁ״י שָׁם ב׳:ה׳, וּבַפְּסִיקְתָא פִּסְקָא מ״ד סִימָן ז׳) עַל פָּסוּק: "עֲקָרָה יָלְדָה שִׁבְעָה וְרַבַּת בָּנִים אֻמְלָלָה" [שְׁמוּאֵל א ב׳:ה׳]. וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי רֹב כַּעַס דְּכִעֲסַתָּה צָרָתָהּ בַּעֲבוּר הַרְּעִמָהּ, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִיא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם נִתְכַּוְּנָה (כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּבָבָא בַתְרָא ט״ז עַמּוּד א׳), מִכָּל מָקוֹם "סְבִיבָיו נִשְׂעֲרָה מְאֹד" (כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בִּיבָמוֹת קכ״א עַמּוּד ב׳); הֻצְרְכָה לִסְבֹּל עֹנֶשׁ בְּעַד שֶׁצִּעֲרַתָּהּ לְפִי שָׁעָה, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה לְטוֹבָתָהּ בֶּאֱמֶת בַּסּוֹף, וּכְמוֹ הַגּוֹנֵב עַל מְנָת לְשַׁלֵּם תַּשְׁלוּמֵי כֶפֶל דְּאָסוּר (כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּבָבָא קַמָּא ס״א עַמּוּד ב׳). וְכָל דִּקְדּוּקָיו עִם הַצַּדִּיקִים וְעִם כְּלַל זֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל הַכֹּל הוּא: "כַּאֲשֶׁר יְיַסֵּר אִישׁ אֶת בְּנוֹ וְגוֹמֵר" [דְּבָרִים ח׳:ה׳], שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הָרַחְמָנוּת, כְּרַחֵם אָב עַל בָּנִים, כְּמוֹ הָעוֹשֶׂה אֵיזֶה צַעַר לִרְפוּאָה. וּכְמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר (עָמוֹס ג׳:ב׳): "רַק אֶתְכֶם יָדַעְתִּי וְגוֹמֵר עַל כֵּן אֶפְקֹד וְגוֹמֵר", וּבְרַחֲמִים מַסִּיק לֵיהּ כְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (ד׳ עַמּוּד א׳), דְּ"יָדַעְתִּי" מִלְּשׁוֹן "מוֹדָע לְאִישָׁהּ" [רוּת ג׳:ב׳], דִּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר אוֹהֵב, עַל כֵּן "אֶפְקֹד" — בִּפְקִידָה וְהַשְׁגָּחָה, לֹא בְּסִלּוּק הַהַשְׁגָּחָה וְעַל יְדֵי הַמְּסִירָה לְדֶרֶךְ הַטֶּבַע שֶׁהִיא בְּגִימַטְרִיָּה שֵׁם "אֱלֹהִים" שֶׁבּוֹ נִדּוֹנִים אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵצֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נֶאֱמַר: "כִּי ה' הוֹגָה" [אֵיכָה א׳:ה׳], וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת בְּסֵפֶר אֵיכָה שֵׁם הֲוָיָ״ה, שֶׁהַכֹּל בְּרַחֲמִים גְּמוּרִים.
records.targetEnglish: This occurred with Hannah, for Peninnah was given in her stead, as our Sages explained the verse “The barren woman has borne seven, and she who had many children languishes” (Midrash Shmuel 5; Rashi on I Samuel 2:5; Pesikta, section 44:7). It came through the great vexation with which her rival provoked her, in order to make her cry out. Although her intention was for the sake of Heaven (Bava Batra 16a), nevertheless “around Him it storms exceedingly” (Yevamot 121b): she had to bear punishment for causing Hannah momentary pain, even though it ultimately truly benefited her. This resembles stealing in order to repay double, which is forbidden (Bava Metzia 61b [editorial correction of the citation in the quoted Hebrew]). All His exacting treatment of the righteous and of the entire seed of Israel follows “as a man disciplines his son”: it comes from mercy, like a father’s compassion for his children or someone causing pain for the sake of healing. As it is said, “You alone have I known … therefore I shall attend to [your sins]” (Amos 3:2); it concludes with mercy, as explained in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (4a). “I have known” is like “a kinsman of her husband,” meaning one who loves. Therefore “I shall attend”—through attention and providence, rather than withdrawing providence and handing them over to the way of nature, whose Hebrew numerical value is that of the name Elohim, through which the nations are judged. By contrast, of the children of Israel it is said, “For the Lord has afflicted her” (Lamentations 1:5), and in several places in Lamentations the name Havayah is used, for everything is in complete mercy.
records.explanation: Poked Akarim uses the same father-and-child verse to explain Divine correction as attentive mercy, comparable to healing. Its treatment of Peninnah immediately before that explanation keeps an essential distinction visible: a beneficial eventual outcome and a pious intention do not excuse the human act of causing pain. This clarifies the kind of assistance discussed in Lech Lecha and its following prayer for merciful, light correction. Citation note: the quoted Hebrew names Bava Kamma 61b; the passage about stealing in order to repay double is in Bava Metzia 61b.

records.themeTitle: How an obstacle becomes assistance
records.themeSummary: The opposite of outward ease can also aid service. Tiferet Yosef explains this through obstacles whose eventual help is discovered by working through them.
records.originHebrew: וּבְאִם לָאו חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, יִהְיוּ הַסִּיַּיעְתָּא לְקִיּוּם מִצְווֹתָיו עַל יְדֵי הַהֵיפֶךְ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם; וְהַהֵיפֶךְ הוּא גַּם כֵּן לְעֵזֶר, שֶׁנּוּכַל לְהִתְגַּבֵּר וְלִכְבּוֹשׁ אֶת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע. וְזֶהוּ: "יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּטַח בַּה', עֶזְרָם וּמָגִנָּם הוּא".
records.originEnglish: If not, God forbid, the assistance toward keeping His mitzvot will come through the opposite, God forbid. That opposite is also help, so that we can grow stronger and subdue the evil inclination. This is “Israel, trust in the Lord; He is their help and their shield.”
records.targetHebrew:
ויאמר ד' אלהים לא טוב היות האדם לבדו.
ביאר בזה כבוד אאמו"ר זללה"ה שמה שייך אצל השי"ת שרק עכשיו ראה שלא טוב היות אדם לבדו, ומקודם הבריאה לא ראה זאת. רק הענין בזה, דזה עצמו היה בריאה מן השי"ת שלאדם לא ימצא לו עזר, דהיינו שבתפיסתו בל ימצא לו עזר. וכמו שביאר בזה כבוד אזמו"ר זללה"ה אעשה לו עזר כנגדו, היינו אצל הבריאה הוא כל עזר מדבר שכנגדו, היינו שהציב השי"ת לאדם כל מיני מניעות והאדם הולך ומרחיב כבוד שמים ומסלק ממנו כל המניעות, ומחזיר את כל הדברים פנים בפנים להשי"ת, ואז רואה האדם שיש לו מן אלו המניעות כל הסיעתות. וכמו דאיתא בש"ס (בבא מציעא פ"ד.) מעיקרא כי הוה אמר ר' יוחנן מילי הוה מקשי ליה ריש לקיש עשרים וארבעה קושייתא [ומפרק ליה רבי יוחנן עשרים וארבעה פירוקי] וממילא רווחא שמעתא. והיינו שהציב השי"ת שכל הסיעתות לא יהיה רק מן דבר שכנגדו, וזה זכה עזר לא זכה כנגדו, זכה היינו אם מתגבר על כל אלו המניעות ומסלק ממנו, אז רואה שיש לו כל הסיעתות וזה עזר, ואם לא ח"ו אז כנגדו:
records.targetEnglish: “The Lord God said: It is not good for the human being to be alone.” My revered father explained: how could it apply to the blessed God that only now He saw it was not good for the human being to be alone, and did not see it before creation? Rather, this itself was a creation from God: the human being would find no help—that is, in his perception he would find no help. As my revered grandfather explained “I shall make him a helper opposite him”: within creation, every help comes from something that stands opposite. God placed every kind of obstacle before the person, and the person goes on expanding the honor of Heaven, removing the obstacles, and turning everything face to face toward God. Then he sees that all these obstacles supply assistance. Thus the Talmud says (Bava Metzia 84a) that originally, when Rabbi Yochanan stated a teaching, Resh Lakish would raise twenty-four objections [and Rabbi Yochanan would resolve them with twenty-four answers], and consequently the teaching became broader. God established that all assistance would come from something opposing. This is “If he merits, a help; if he does not merit, opposite him.” If he merits—if he overcomes and removes all those obstacles—he sees that he has every assistance: this is a help. Otherwise, God forbid, it remains opposite him.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef gives a concrete model for calling an opposing circumstance help: Resh Lakish’s questions initially confront a teaching, and working through them broadens its understanding. The same passage retains the condition of overcoming the obstacles; without that work, the opposition remains opposition. This explains how Lech Lecha can call difficult circumstances assistance toward conquering the inclination, without making difficulty itself an accomplished spiritual gain.
